activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: At 7 percent annual growth compounded yearly, $1,000 grows to almost $15,000 in forty years, so money saved at eighteen can multiply many times by retirement.
story:
The screen door banged twice behind Jacob, once for his backpack and once for him, and his grandfather looked up from the kitchen table where he was sorting envelopes into two piles. It was the first humid week of July, and Jacob had come to spend the weekend partly because his mother had asked and partly because his grandfather's house had the only quiet porch left in the family. He set his first-ever paycheck on the table, face up, like a fish he had caught and wanted weighed.

"Four hundred and twelve dollars," his grandfather said, reading without touching it. "Not bad for bagging groceries."

"Three weeks of smelling like cantaloupe," Jacob said. "There's a kid there, Alexandre from my chemistry class, he does the same job and spends every cent on sneakers. He denigrates the whole idea of saving. Says it's for people with no imagination." He watched his grandfather's hands move an envelope marked with a red stamp from one pile to the other, then back, as if deciding something.

His grandfather only grunted at that, which Jacob had learned was not disagreement but thinking. "Come here a minute," he said finally, and pulled a thin green folder from the drawer under the phone nook, the drawer that held the shoehorn and the dead pens. Inside was a single page, a bank statement from so long ago the logo had a different shape. "I want you to look at something and tell me what you see."

Jacob read the numbers twice. A deposit of one thousand dollars, made when his grandfather was barely older than Alexandre was now, and beside it, forty years later, a figure just under fifteen thousand. He felt the peculiar vertigo of a thing clicking into place, like the first time he'd understood that the stars were not small. "This is the same thousand?" he asked. "It just sat there?"

"Seven percent a year, compounded yearly," his grandfather said, tapping the paper with one crooked finger. "The bank man told me that in 1970-something and I didn't believe him either."

Jacob did the arithmetic on the back of an electric bill with a pencil stub, because his phone was upstairs charging and because something about the folder demanded pencil. He wrote the number fifteen thousand and circled it, then wrote fifty-eight, the age his grandfather would have been, then wrote his own fifty-eight, forty years from this July. The same math, if it held, if nothing went wrong, if the world kept its promises. He kept writing "if" in the margin until the letters looked like a picket fence.

Later that evening Zara came over, riding her bike the three blocks from her grandmother's place with a container of empanadas balanced in the handlebar basket, because she had heard about the paycheck and considered any occasion involving money one that required food. She sat on the porch steps and listened to him explain the green folder, the thousand, the fifteen thousand, the forty years, and the sneakers Alexandre had bought and already scuffed.

"So the money you save at eighteen is basically a different amount by retirement," she said slowly, working it through. "It multiplies. That's almost unfair. That's almost beautiful."

"That's what I said. Except." Jacob leaned back against the porch post. "Except the world might not hold still for forty years, and seven percent might not be what it is then, and Alexandre's sneakers make him happy now, which is also a real thing. I keep trying to hold both of them in my head at once and they don't fit in the same hand."

"You're allowed to not know," Zara said, with the flat sagacity of someone who had decided this about herself two years earlier and found it comfortable. "You could split it. Some saved, some sneakers. That's not a compromise, that's just being a person."

The porch light came on automatically, as it did every evening at eight-fifteen, and moths began their grandiose looping flights against it, falling and rising like they were rehearsing something they would never perform. Jacob thought about his grandfather's two piles of envelopes, the way he had moved one back and forth. He thought about Ms. Sánchez next door, who had once told him over the fence that she wished she'd started her retirement account at eighteen instead of thirty-five, and how she'd said it lightly, the way people say things they've made peace with and haven't.

"Monday," he said, "when the bank's open, I'm going to ask them what a kid with four hundred and twelve dollars can do. Not because I believe the fifteen thousand is guaranteed. Because I'd rather be the kind of person who ran the numbers than the kind who didn't."

"That's the least romantic sentence you've ever spoken," Zara said, and stole an empanada.

Inside, through the screen, his grandfather could be seen sitting at the kitchen table again, moving one envelope slowly from the red-stamp pile to the other pile, and holding it there, as though testing the weight of some decision whose answer would not arrive for forty years. Jacob watched him set it down at last and reach for his reading glasses.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: One month of free rent on a twelve-month lease at 1,200 dollars a month lowers the effective monthly rent to 1,100 dollars.
story:
The line at the bank was six deep and barely moving, which gave Layla time to spread both leases across the counter ledge by the deposit slips. She had come to open her first checking account, the one her mother had said she'd need before August, but the paperwork had taken ten minutes and now the teller was with someone disputing a fee, so she stood to the side with her folder and let the building's cold air settle on her shoulders. Ashley had texted her an hour ago: which one, tell me which one, I need to know by tonight.

The first lease was at Marbury Court, eleven hundred a month, no special, utilities listed separately. The second was at a complex on Delmore Street, twelve hundred a month, with a banner across its website that said ONE MONTH FREE. Ashley was set on the Delmore place because of the pool and because one month free sounded, in her words, like winning something. Layla had gone along with that logic until this morning, when she'd read the fine print twice on the bus and felt the arithmetic going soft in her head, which was why she'd brought the papers everywhere, including here.

"Are you in line?" said a voice beside her. Austyn, from her economics class, holding a check and a phone with a cracked screen. He glanced at the pages under her hands. "Moving out?"

"In theory. Two apartments, one decision." She straightened the pages so he could see if he wanted to, and he did want to, because Austyn read everything, even other people's mail if they let him. "The Delmore one is twelve hundred but you don't pay for one month out of the twelve."

Austyn frowned at the banner she'd printed out. "So it's cheaper overall."

"That's what Ashley says." Layla pulled a pen from her folder and, on the back of a deposit slip, wrote 12 times 1200, then subtracted 1200. Thirteen thousand two hundred minus twelve hundred was twelve thousand over the year. She divided by twelve and the number that came up was eleven hundred a month, exactly the same as Marbury's rent before utilities, the same as the place with no pool and no banner. She looked at it a long moment. "It's not cheaper. One month free on a twelve-month lease at twelve hundred a month brings it down to eleven hundred a month. Same as the boring one."

"That's a little evil," Austyn said, almost admiring.

"Or it's just marketing." But it didn't feel the same as the boring one, and that was the part Layla couldn't turn into a number. The free month was at signing, the manager had told her, so September would cost her nothing while she was buying a mattress and dishes and a shower curtain, when money was thinnest. Marbury spread everything evenly, month after month, no gift and no gap. She wrote both columns anyway, rent on one side, the utilities row underneath, because the Delmore place included water and trash while Marbury charged for both, and those numbers were real too, fifteen dollars here, thirty there, small enough to seem like nothing until they reified a whole apartment into a cost she would owe every single month.

She thought about her mother, who distrusted anything advertised loudly and had once spent forty minutes on the phone with a landlord in a voice Layla could only call vitriolic over a broken garbage disposal. Her mother would say the banner was a trick. Her economics teacher, Mr. Cohen, had a different line he repeated, that a thing's cost and a thing's price were two different animals, and Layla had rolled her eyes at it in class and now heard it in his slow voice at this counter as if he were standing behind her. The two apartments cost the same in rent. They did not cost the same in cash flow, or in utilities, or in what it would feel like to write a check for nothing in September and a full check every month after.

The teller called next in line and Austyn stepped up, sliding his check through the slot, and Layla heard the cashier's window open beside her for her own deposit. She finished it quickly, the new account now holding the four hundred dollars she'd saved from the bookstore job, and while the teller counted bills, Ashley's name lit up the phone again: the manager at Delmore is showing a unit at 5, did you decide.

Outside, the afternoon had gone amber at the edges, the parking lot shimmering. Layla sat on the low concrete wall by the doors and typed, then deleted, then typed again. Not the cheaper one, she wrote. They come out the same, 1100 either way with the free month. Then, before she could second-guess it: go look at both. Check what utilities cost. I'll meet you at Delmore at 5 and we'll ask about water and trash before you sign anything. She stood, folded the leases into the folder, and started the walk toward Delmore Street with the deposit slips still in her pocket, the arithmetic side facing out, eleven hundred written twice.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: Melodies are often built from four-bar phrases, so a sixteen-bar melody commonly falls into four phrases.
story:
James sat in the back of the music room with the assignment sheet flat on the desk. Sixteen bars, melody with chord changes, written in standard notation, due Friday. Mr. Ramos had said the deadline was firm, though he also granted amnesty to anyone who stayed after school to work, which meant the deadline was firm only if you refused the offer. James had refused it for two days. Today he pushed his chair back, found a sheet of staff paper, and drew sixteen empty bars across four systems.

He had a first bar he liked: a small rise from B to D, the kind of thing that sounded like someone deciding to go outside. Bar two answered it. Bar three repeated it lower. Then bar four did nothing he wanted, and neither did bar five, and by bar six the page looked like a field after a bad harvest. He wrote numbers above the bars, then crossed them out, then wrote them again. The room smelled of valve oil and the radiator's dry heat, and somewhere in the hall a tuba player worked the same three notes over and over, which did not portend anything good for anyone's concentration.

Nova came in with a sandwich half eaten in her hand and sat down across from him without asking. She wanted the window seat, which he had taken because the light was better for pencil work, and she wanted it enough to argue about it.

"You know I can't write with that glare on the left side," she said.

"Trade you my manuscript paper," James said. "I have eleven sheets left."

"Twelve sheets and the window."

"Eleven and the pencil sharpener."

They settled on eleven sheets and she took the sharpener. She was ahead of him, eleven bars done, and she kept turning her page so he could see that. Her melody was all big leaps and drama, a thing she called storm music, and she had spent their last class on a tangential argument about whether minor keys were sadder than slow tempos, which had eaten twenty minutes and produced no bars at all.

Mr. Ramos drifted over and looked at James's page for a long moment without touching it. "How's the shape coming?"

"It isn't," James said. "I've got four bars. Then it stops."

"Play me the four."

James played them on the upright piano against the wall. The rise, the answer, the repeat lower. Mr. Ramos listened with his arms folded, nodded once, and moved on to the tuba player in the hall, which James understood as a verdict of not yet rather than no.

He stared at the four bars. It occurred to him, slowly, the way things occur when you stop trying to force them, that four bars was not a fragment. Four bars was a whole thought, a phrase that had said its piece and stopped. He looked down the page at the twelve empty bars and thought of them not as one long road but as three more thoughts. Bar five could begin again, the way bar one had, but changed. He wrote the rise again and moved the answer up a third. Nine bars were still blank, and they no longer looked blank so much as waiting.

"Wait," Nova said, leaning over. "You're just doing the same thing four times?"

"Not the same." He played her the first phrase, then the second. "Like sentences. You say something, you say it back different, then something new, then you bring it around."

Nova pulled her own sheet toward her and counted her eleven bars with a pencil tip. She frowned at them, drew a bracket after her fourth bar, and another after her eighth. "Mine's all one run-on," she said. "Ramos is going to write 'breathe' on it in red pen." She started cutting, moving two of her big leaps into a fresh fifth bar and inventing an ending for the first phrase out of the last note she'd had. The tuba in the hall had stopped. The radiator ticked.

By the end of the period James had all sixteen bars, four phrases, the third one going somewhere new and the fourth coming back to B, with chord letters penciled under each change and one rough spot in bar fourteen he circled to fix tomorrow. Nova had twelve bars she liked better than her original eleven and took the window seat anyway when he packed up, claiming it as her fee for the advice.

"What do you do for the last phrase?" she asked, gathering her storm music. "Do you end it or leave it hanging?"

"I don't know yet," James said. He clipped his sheet into his folder. "I'll know when I play it for him."

"Cheater. You're supposed to know before you play it."

James zipped his bag. "Then tomorrow I'll listen harder than I know."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
story:
Morgan tied the scarf under her chin in the car mirror twice, and it looked wrong twice, like a badly wrapped parcel. In the back seat, Isabelle watched her do it.

"So I just keep this on the whole time," Isabelle said.

"Everyone covers their head. It's a sign of respect." Morgan's mother pulled into the lot of the gurdwara, where her uncle was already waiting by the doors in a turquoise kurta, waving like a man hailing a ship. It was her cousin Jasleen's Anand Karaj, the wedding, and the whole extended family had driven in from three states, which meant an afternoon of aunts commenting on Morgan's weight, her hair, her college plans, in that order.

"And you're sure I'm allowed in? I'm, like, extremely not Sikh."

"You're allowed. Trust me."

Morgan had explained the basics in the parking lot of their school two weeks ago, a pithy little speech she'd rehearsed: shoes off, head covered, no pointing your feet at the Guru Granth Sahib, and don't photograph anything until someone says you can. What she had not explained, because her grandmother had explained it to her only once and long ago, was the meal afterward. She had been seven the first time, sulking because she'd wanted pizza, and her grandmother had set her down on the floor of the langar hall between strangers and said, "Look. Everyone sits here. The same. Rich, poor, doesn't matter." Morgan had mostly remembered the rice pudding. She had eaten four servings and been sick in the parking lot, which her family still brought up at every wedding, a story with the half-life of uranium.

Inside, the hall smelled of cardamom and hot oil. They found seats near the back, and Morgan's aunt arrived within ninety seconds, glancing at Isabelle with the polite suspicion of a customs officer. "And who is this?"

"Isabelle. From school."

"From school," the aunt repeated, as if Morgan had said from the moon. She looked at Isabelle's scarf, which was actually a very nice scarf, and moved on to interrogate Morgan about whether she was eating enough, and then about whether she was eating too much, the two questions occupying the same aunt in the same breath.

The ceremony was long and beautiful and, Morgan had to admit, mostly opaque to her. She understood the shape of it and not the words, and she spent part of it watching Isabelle, who was leaning forward with an attention Morgan found almost embarrassing. There was a moment when the ragis sang and the whole hall went still, and Isabelle glanced over, and Morgan mouthed, I know, and Isabelle nodded like she actually did.

Afterward came the meal, and this was the part Morgan had been half-dreading, not because it would be bad but because she'd had to argue for it. In the car that morning her father had said the hall would be chaotic, two hundred relatives, and Isabelle would feel out of place, and maybe they should drop her home first. Morgan had said no with a force that surprised her, and the argument had ossified into a silence that lasted through most of the drive, her father's hands at ten and two, her mother looking out the window. Morgan hadn't been able to say why it mattered. Only that it did.

The langar hall had rows of mats laid out on the floor, and people sat cross-legged in lines, servers moving between them with steel buckets, ladling dal and rice onto every tray, one after another after another. Morgan's uncle from Texas, who owned four car dealerships and referred to himself as self-made at least once per visit, sat on the floor beside a man in a road-worker's vest, and neither of them was above the other, because the floor did not permit it. There was no head table, no family table, no special anything.

"This is langar," Morgan said quietly, as they folded down onto the mats. "The free kitchen. It's vegetarian, it's free, and it's for anyone. Any religion, any caste, doesn't matter who you are. You just sit on the floor with everyone."

"On the floor."

"On the floor. Everyone. That's the whole point."

Isabelle looked down the row. Morgan's grandmother was further along, directing a volunteer toward the spot beside her, patting the mat. When she spotted Isabelle, she patted it again, twice, an imperial gesture.

"Is she," Isabelle began.

"Yes. Go."

They ate. Isabelle, who Morgan knew for a fact had once eaten cold noodles out of a vending machine at midnight rather than speak to a cashier, talked to her grandmother about, of all things, gardening, and her grandmother, who had told Morgan her English was not so good, conducted the entire conversation in fluid, opinionated English and laughed at her own jokes. Morgan sat two mats down and watched this happen with a feeling she could not immediately file. Something about the version of her grandmother that existed for strangers, or the version of her family that existed outside the car, outside the aunts and the questions about weight and college. Her father found her there with a cup of chai.

"You didn't drop her home," he said.

"No."

He looked down the row at his mother-in-law and Isabelle, heads together over a tray.

"Perspicacity," Morgan said. "Look it up."

"I know what it means." He sipped the chai. He was quiet for a moment, and she could see him deciding whether to be the person from the car or some other person, and the decision not landing anywhere yet. Her grandmother was showing Isabelle how to fold her scarf properly, hands moving, not explaining, just doing it, and Isabelle was copying her with the concentration of someone defusing a bomb.

"More rice, beta?" her father said finally, and lifted the bucket before Morgan could answer.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
The pan had defeated Chase twice already, and it was not going to defeat him a third time. The first attempt at Grandma's kitchen had produced chicken the color of someone who had never once seen sunlight, pale and sweating on a plate while his grandfather ate it anyway, out of love or obstinacy, and said it was "very moist." Which was true the way a puddle was very moist. The second attempt he had overcorrected, cranked the burner to its highest setting, and filled the kitchen with a smoke sharp enough to sensitize everyone's eyes for the rest of the evening, so that even Robert, who had laughed the hardest, spent twenty minutes blinking at the ceiling fan like a man in a silent film.

Now it was Saturday, and the whole crew had migrated to the grandparents' house for what Cassandre kept calling "the rematch." She had appointed herself judge, Robert had appointed himself commentator, and Chase had appointed himself the only person actually willing to touch raw poultry. His grandfather sat at the table with a crossword, pretending to be above it all, though his pencil had not moved in ten minutes.

"Third time's the charm," Robert said from the counter, where he was tearing lettuce with the casual violence of someone who considered salad a betrayal. "Or third time's the smoke alarm, which honestly has more entertainment value."

"You're an aesthete," Cassandre told him. "You only like things that are dramatic."

"I'm an aesthete," Robert agreed, "which is why pale chicken offends me spiritually."

Chase laid the thighs in the pan skin-side down and watched them do exactly what they had done before: sit there, grey and patient, releasing water, steaming in their own juices. It was like watching a bathtub fill while you were trying to fry an egg. He stared at the liquid pooling around the meat and felt the tectonic shift of an idea grinding into place. Steaming. That word. He had been treating heat like a volume knob, louder or quieter, when maybe it was a threshold instead, a door that either opened or didn't.

"Can I see your phone?" he said to Cassandre.

She handed it over, and he typed fast, half sure he was inventing a problem that didn't exist. But there it was, on a cooking site and then a chemistry forum and then, absurdly, in the pinned materials from Mr. Hughes's class page, because apparently Mr. Hughes ran the chemistry club like a cult with a food theme. Cassandre leaned over his shoulder and read aloud, mostly to annoy Robert, who claimed he preferred to receive information as gossip.

"The Maillard reaction," she read, "between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor, and it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius."

"Maillard," Chase said, testing the word.

"Named after a French guy," Robert said. "Everything delicious is named after a French guy. It's a rule."

"Maillard reaction," his grandfather said from the table, without looking up from the crossword, tapping his pencil twice against the pan lid like a man ringing a small bell. Then he went back to seven across, which was either "blunt instrument, five letters" or the entire theme of Chase's morning.

So the water had been the whole problem. All that liquid hissing out of the meat kept the surface cool, kept it steaming somewhere well below where anything interesting could happen. The door never opened. It wasn't that he was a bad cook; it was that he had been asking the pan for the wrong thing. Chase took the chicken out, poured the liquid off, set the pan back down empty, and waited. Robert made a joke about watching paint heat. Cassandre shushed him with a wooden spoon held like a conductor's baton.

When the empty pan shimmered, when a drop of water skated across it and vanished in a breath, he laid the thighs in again, and this time the sound was different, a hard low crackle, and the skin went gold almost at once, then brown, then a deep mahogany at the edges with little blackened blisters. The smell that came up off it was so obviously the smell of everything good he had ever eaten that Cassandre said a word she usually saved for exams, and even Robert stopped tearing lettuce.

They ate on the porch with the screen door banging, the family summoned by scent alone, his grandmother claiming a thigh before anyone could argue. The skin crunched; the meat underneath was still soft, and his grandfather chewed slowly, looking out at the yard, and finally said, "Well. That's the one."

Chase took his plate apart down to the bone and thought about thresholds, about how many other doors he'd been standing in front of, pushing gently, mistaking patience for method. He wasn't sure the lesson carried anywhere beyond the kitchen. He wasn't sure it didn't. Robert stole the last piece of skin off his plate, right off the edge, grinning the whole time, and Chase let him have it.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Truman Doctrine, announced in March 1947, pledged US support for countries resisting communist pressure, starting with aid to Greece and Turkey.
story:
The essay prompt had been sitting in Jacob's bag for six days, unfolded once and then refolded along a different crease: two historians, two explanations of the Cold War's origins, judged against the evidence. He had chosen the public library because his grandfather's house, where he usually worked, had become a place he could no longer think in. He spread his notes across a table near the periodicals, two paperbacks propped open like lawyers presenting rival cases. One historian argued that the Soviets had driven the conflict, expansion by exhaustion on their side and defensive alarm on ours. The other argued that the Americans had needed markets and had dressed that need in the language of freedom, that the rhetoric of containment was a way to inculcate a permanent wartime economy into a country that had just finished a war. Jacob had read both twice. He believed both, which felt like believing nothing.

Oscar arrived with a milkshake he wasn't supposed to have in the building and a thesis of his own, which was that everything came down to money. "Follow the dollars," he said, sliding into the chair across from Jacob. "Greece, Turkey, whoever. The Americans didn't care about democracy, they cared about ports and trade routes."

"You haven't read either of them," Jacob said, but without heat, because Oscar's confidence was a weather system he had learned to work around rather than resist. He laid out his timeline on the table, the events he'd copied onto index cards in his grandfather's neat, slanted hand, and it was here that his certainty wobbled. The cards were chronological up to a point and then, in one place, wrong. He had written the Truman Doctrine speech at 1946, a full year early, and beneath it he'd pencilled the Long Telegram, Kennan's warning from Moscow, at 1947, which was backwards. He stared at the cards for a long moment, sure he had copied them correctly, sure his grandfather had written them correctly, and unable for the moment to hold both certainties at once.

Mr. Ndlovu passed with a trolley of returns and paused, because pausing was his way of offering help without intruding on anyone's dignity. He noticed the milkshake. He did not mention the milkshake. He noticed the cards. "The reference shelf," he said, tapping the air above the timeline, "has the documents themselves. Speeches, telegrams. Originals beat arguments, in my experience. Historians are advocates; the documents are only witnesses, and witnesses can be cross-examined." Then he moved on toward the display case he was preparing for the library's seventy-fifth anniversary, which he had wanted for years to be his and which the board kept voting to postpone, and which he had finally been granted three weeks to assemble, a deadline that mattered to him more than any teenage essayist could know.

Morgane had been watching from the study carrels, not eavesdropping exactly but unable not to hear, the way one cannot not hear a wrong note. She came over with her own stack of books, debate-prep material, because in two weeks she would compete in the regional finals and she wanted, with a specificity that kept her up at night, to beat the school that had eliminated her last year on a Cold War question she had fumbled. She wanted this timeline to be right because her outline was built on it. She wanted, in a quieter way she hadn't said aloud, to be the person who knew things first.

"Your dates are flipped," she said, and pointed, and Jacob felt the unfair swell of irritation that precedes being corrected.

"I know what I wrote," he said, and then, because Mr. Ndlovu had already told him where the shelf was, he went anyway.

The volume of speeches was heavier than he expected and smelled of dust and someone else's decade. He found March 1947. He read the speech itself, Truman asking Congress for money, and the aid was for Greece and Turkey first, those two countries named plainly, the support pledged for any country resisting communist pressure. He carried the volume back like a verdict. "The Truman Doctrine, March 1947," he said, setting the book down between Oscar and Morgane, open to the page. "Pledged US support for countries resisting communist pressure. Aid to Greece and Turkey first. That's the start, not the Long Telegram, not 1946. I had it backwards."

"So the revisionist's wrong," Oscar said at once, already rewriting the essay in his head, already satisfied. Jacob almost let him. It was easier to let the correction flip him from one camp into the other, orthodox into revisionist and back again, the way his grandfather had always flipped between deciding a question was settled and deciding everyone who'd settled it was a fool.

But Morgane leaned over the speech, finger on the page, and said the thing Jacob had been circling without landing on. "It doesn't tell you why he pledged it." She looked up. "It tells you what he said. The other guy tells you why. They're not actually disagreeing about the speech."

The library's afternoon light had gone long and low across the tables, and Mr. Ndlovu was lifting a glass pane into the display case with both hands, holding his breath, sliding it into its channel. Jacob sat down. He took out a fresh card and wrote the doctrine on one side of it, 1947, Greece and Turkey, the facts as the documents gave them, and on the other side he wrote the two historians' questions and found they were not the same question at all. One asked what the Soviets did. The other asked what the Americans wanted. The speech answered the first and left the second standing there, waiting, and Jacob understood that his essay would have to say that, would have to end where the evidence ended, in the honest blank space where he still could not choose.

It was only then, copying the corrected card in his grandfather's slant without meaning to, that he let himself remember the argument at the kitchen table two months before the funeral, his grandfather insisting the telegram was the real start, insisting with a certainty Jacob now knew was simply wrong. He had died certain. Jacob held the card a moment longer, the milkshake sweating a ring onto the wood beside it, and then Morgane said, "Read me the Turkey part again, I want the exact words," and slid her outline across the table toward him.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
Nicolas had been eighteen for exactly three weeks, which felt like the difference between standing outside a building and standing inside it, holding a ticket he wasn't sure how to use. The line at the school gymnasium moved slowly, and Adelaide stood beside him in her green canvas jacket, holding her voter card the way other people held phones at funerals.

"You're voting for Harrow, right?" she said. It wasn't quite a question. She had campaigned for Harrow since September, stapling flyers to telephone poles in the rain, and she wanted, he understood, not just his vote but his agreement, the pleasure of being agreed with. Nicolas had spent two evenings with the sample ballots spread on his bedroom floor, and the truth was messier than she would have liked: he admired Harrow's housing plan but distrusted the budget behind it, and he admired the other candidate's honesty while doubting her numbers.

"I'm still deciding," he said.

"It's a truism that the perfect candidate doesn't exist," Adelaide said, a little too briskly, as though quoting her own campaign literature. "So you pick the one who'll actually build the apartments."

Russell was ahead of them in the line, saturnine as always, arms crossed, radiating the opinion that the whole ceremony was theatre. "You know nobody watches you mark it," he said when they shuffled forward. "There's a reason for that."

"Because they don't care?" Adelaide said.

"Because it's secret. It has a name. The Australian ballot." He said it flatly, like a password. "The Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, brought it in. 1856." He shrugged. "Before that, people could see how you voted. Then they couldn't."

Nicolas turned this over. He had assumed the little cardboard screens were furniture, some bureaucratic habit, but they were an invention, argued for and won, exported around the world. It meant his decision, whatever it became, would belong to no one but him. Not Adelaide, who had earned his loyalty in the rain; not his father, who had announced at dinner that any vote for Harrow was a vote for fiscal fantasy; not Russell, who would call him a dupe either way.

Inside the gym, Ms. Lau, who taught him chemistry two years ago and now worked the registration table, found his name in the binder. "First time," she said, not a question either, and slid the ballot across. "Booth's on the left."

The booth smelled of pencil shavings. Nicolas stood with the stubby pencil hovering, and the two perspectives he'd been carrying all month settled beside each other like people at a bus stop: Adelaide's argument that imperfect action beat pure hesitation, and his father's argument that a promise you can't pay for is a lie wearing a suit. Neither had the whole truth. What he could see clearly was narrower and more his own: Harrow's plan would help people in three years if it survived, and the other candidate's caution would help no one but would harm no one. He thought of Russell's flat little history lesson, that the screens existed because someone had decided a vote should be answerable only to the person casting it. That was the part he hadn't expected to matter. Whatever he chose, he would have to live inside it alone.

He marked the box, folded the paper along its creases, and carried it to the box where a woman with a badge watched each ballot drop, one by one, like deposits at a bank that paid no interest.

Outside, Adelaide was waiting on the low wall, and he could see the question forming on her face before he reached her. "Well?" she said.

"That's the whole point," Nicolas said. "I don't have to tell you."

She looked at him for a long moment, and something shifted in her expression, not anger exactly, more like recalibration, as if she were deciding whether a friend who kept his own counsel was better than one who acceded. "Fine," she said finally. "Then tell me this. Did it feel like it mattered?"

Russell came out the doors behind them, zipping his jacket, and paused on the steps, listening.

"I don't know yet," Nicolas said. "Ask me in four years."

Adelaide laughed once, surprised out of her campaign posture, and Russell shook his head at both of them, already walking toward the bus stop, hands deep in his pockets.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
Rosalie got to the ice cream shop ten minutes early, which she decided was worse than being late, because now she had to stand alone under the menu board pretending to study flavors she already knew. Ethen had asked her out on Thursday, in the parking lot, in a voice so casual it must have been rehearsed, and she had said yes before she had finished deciding whether she wanted to. That was the problem with saying things quickly. You had to spend the next three days catching up to your own mouth.

He arrived only two minutes after her, hair still damp from a shower, holding the door for a woman with a stroller who didn't acknowledge him. "I was going to walk here," he said, "but then I thought, what if I arrive all sweaty and out of breath. Bad first impression."

"Depends," Rosalie said. "There's this study from 1974, by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron. Men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge."

Ethen blinked. "What?"

"That's it. That's the whole thing. If you'd shown up sweaty and terrified, I might have found you more attractive. Apparently you can't always tell the difference between being scared and liking someone. Or the study couldn't, anyway. The men couldn't." She hadn't meant to open with it. But Ms. Nowak had told their psych class about it on Friday, offhand, during a unit they'd already been tested on, and Rosalie had gone home and read the original article twice, partly because it was interesting and partly because she suspected it was about her.

They ordered. Ethen got a double cone with two incompatible flavors, which she chose not to read anything into, and she got a single scoop of the pistachio that turned out to be almost flavorless. The girl behind the counter, whose nametag said Kale, was counting the drawer and being quietly, pointedly efficient about it, the way people are when they've been told to close in forty minutes and customers keep coming.

"So wait," Ethen said, settling into the booth across from her. "The guys on the scary bridge thought they liked her? Because their hearts were pounding?"

"Maybe. Or their hearts were pounding and they decided it was about her. The study doesn't say. That's what I keep noticing about it, is how much it doesn't say." She turned her spoon over in the melting green. She had a memory she kept circling back to, the fall talent show, when she'd been backstage with her hands shaking before her piano piece and a boy in the wings had told her she looked great, and she'd thought about him for a month afterward. She had internalized that month as evidence. Now she held the same memory up to the light and couldn't tell what it was evidence of.

"I hate that," Ethen said, but he was grinning. "I hate that there's no sturdy-bridge version of me to compare you to."

"There isn't a sturdy-bridge version of anything. That's what's annoying. You can't run yourself twice."

From the counter, Kale called over, not unfriendly: "You can't run anything twice, but you can order fast, because I close at nine and my manager is a charlatan who'll dock me if the register's even a penny off." She was wiping down the machine already, with a kind of fierce hope, like someone who wanted the shop empty so badly she was trying to empty it by force of wiping. Rosalie understood wanting your shift to end more than you wanted anything the shift contained.

"You play piano, right?" Ethen asked. "My mom saw you at that thing in the fall."

"That thing" was the talent show, and he'd been there too, then, somewhere in the dark. She thought of the shaking hands, the wings, the boy whose name she would not say out loud on this date. "I got through it," she said. "I almost didn't. My hands were shaking so hard I thought I'd miss the octave." And she had liked that feeling, afterward, the whole ride home she had liked it, and she still didn't know if she'd liked playing or liked being terrified or liked the boy in the wings, and the study with its two bridges and its one interviewer sat there in her mind like a question with the answer torn off.

"So if I asked you out again," Ethen said, working on the cone now, "would it be because of the pistachio or because of this conversation?"

"Neither. Or both. I honestly can't tell you which bridge I'm on."

He laughed, a real one, surprised. Kale flipped her cloth over her shoulder and gave them the look of someone making a decision. "Nine means nine," she said, and turned the sign around in the window.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The STAR method answers interview questions about past behavior by describing a Situation, the Task required, the Action you took, and the Result.
story:
The interview was on Thursday at four, at the coffee shop two bus stops from the lake, and Landon had never had a job before, so on Wednesday evening he sat with Bianca and Chiara on the dock behind the canoe shed and asked them what people actually asked you in an interview.

"They ask about your past behavior," Bianca said. She had worked at a bakery the summer before. "My manager told me they like stories with a shape. It's called the STAR method. Situation, Task, Action, Result. You lay out what happened, what you had to do, what you actually did, and how it turned out."

Chiara, dangling her feet over the water, said, "So practice one. Tell a story about something that went wrong."

Landon worked at the day camp as a junior counselor, unpaid except for a stipend the camp called an apportionment of the program budget, forty dollars a week handed over in an envelope on Fridays. He had stories. The one he chose was the talent show from two weeks earlier, when a virulent stomach bug had gone through the campers and taken out both of the senior counselors on the same afternoon, leaving Landon in charge of a stage, a sound system nobody had tested, and eleven acts.

"Situation," he said. "Half the staff was sick. Task: run the talent show anyway. Action: I got the oldest campers to run the music table and I moved the whole thing outside so we wouldn't need the microphone."

"And the result?" Bianca said.

"The result was it worked. Everybody clapped. It was great."

Chiara stopped swinging her feet. "That's not what happened. The speaker in the barn still didn't work, and the whole thing ran without any music at all until I ran to the office and got the little karaoke machine. You were kind of frozen, actually. You were just standing there."

"It ran without music for ten minutes," Landon said. "That's not the same as frozen."

"It was fifteen. I counted."

They argued about it until the sky went orange over the far shore, and Bianca finally said, "Tell the story the honest way tomorrow and see how it sounds," and Landon said he would, though privately he planned to interpolate the karaoke rescue so smoothly that the owner would never notice who had done it.

Thursday afternoon he took the bus in his one collared shirt. The coffee shop smelled like burnt espresso and floor cleaner, and the woman behind the counter had him sit at a small table by the window while she untangled a delivery box between questions. She asked him why he wanted the job, and he said money for college applications, and she nodded without looking up. Then she said, "Tell me about a time a project went wrong and what you did about it."

Landon began the way he had rehearsed. Situation: the stomach bug, the missing counselors, the talent show. Task: make it happen anyway. Action: delegating the music table, moving everything outdoors. He was building toward the result, the version where it worked, where everyone clapped, when he heard himself pause and realized the owner had stopped untying the box and was watching him.

"Then the speaker didn't work," he said. "The one thing I hadn't checked. And for about fifteen minutes I stood there doing nothing, which I didn't plan to tell you, but it's the truth. Another counselor ran and got a backup. The show went on. I'd like to say I learned to test equipment first, and I did learn that, but the bigger thing I learned is that I don't always know which part is going to break."

The owner folded the box flat and set it against the wall. "You know the karaoke machine was my daughter's," she said. "She goes to that camp. She was in the magic act, the one with the playing cards. She said the whole thing was her favorite day of the summer."

Landon blinked. He had watched the magic act from the back of the crowd, a small girl in a purple cape fanning cards at the audience with no music behind her, and he had not known she was connected to anything. He had spent two weeks thinking of that afternoon as his failure, filed away under things to spin better next time.

"There's a Saturday shift and two after-school shifts," the owner said. "Saturdays you'd start at six-thirty, which is earlier than you think it is. You'd be on the register and then dishes when it slows down. Can you handle the register?"

"I can learn it," Landon said.

She slid a form across the table, and a pen, and went back to the counter to serve a man in a golf shirt who wanted a large with room. Outside the window the bus pulled up, his bus, and Landon filled in his name in block letters and watched it idle there while he wrote, half his mind on the form and half on the dock, where he would have to tell Chiara tomorrow that she had been right about the fifteen minutes. The bus left without him. He finished the form, signed it, and pushed it back across the table.

"Six-thirty Saturday," the owner said. "Wear closed-toe shoes."

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Paul Graham's 2008 essay 'How to Disagree' ranks disagreement in seven levels, from name-calling at the bottom to refuting the other person's central point at the top.
story:
The interview was at the community center on Fell Street, in a room with a folding table, two chairs, and a poster about storm drains that had been there so long the sun had bleached it to a rumor. Annabelle sat with her hands in her lap and her phone silenced in her pocket, where it buzzed anyway, twice, like a wasp against glass. The buzzing was the group chat, which had been at war since eleven the night before over whether the spring volunteer day should be at the river cleanup or the food bank. Or rather, it had stopped being about that around midnight, when Walid had told Mason that Mason's opinions were a personality disorder with wifi.

"You're Annabelle," said the woman behind the table, checking a paper. "Ms. Rowe. Thanks for coming in early."

"Thanks for having me." It came out too formal, like a voicemail greeting, and Annabelle felt her ears go warm.

Ms. Rowe worked at the center part time and taught a class across town; Annabelle knew this because she had looked her up at one in the morning, between reading the chat and writing a message she never sent. Ms. Rowe asked the usual things, why she wanted the youth weekend assistant job, what her availability was, and Annabelle answered them in complete sentences that surprised her with their steadiness. Then Ms. Rowe leaned back.

"Here's a scenario. Two volunteers are fighting in the group chat about an event. Insults flying. It's midnight. You're the assistant. What do you do?"

The phone buzzed again in her pocket. Annabelle almost laughed. "That's not hypothetical for me. That's my last six hours."

"Tell me."

She told it plainly, in order, because the order was the thing. Mason wanted the river cleanup because they'd done the food bank two years running and it felt, his word, parochial, same ten kids moving cans in the same basement. Walid wanted the food bank because the river cleanup was mostly photo ops, gloves and grins, and the actual trash got hauled by the city crew the next morning anyway. Somewhere around message forty the argument stopped being about rivers or cans and became about who was a fraud and who was a child, and everyone else went quiet in the way people go quiet at a party when a glass breaks.

"So what would you do," Ms. Rowe said.

Annabelle had found the essay two months ago, during a different fight, when Mason had pasted the link with the message "read this before you type." It was by a man named Paul Graham, from 2008, called "How to Disagree," and it ranked disagreement in levels, seven of them. Name-calling was at the bottom, and the top level was refuting the other person's central point, actually taking their main argument apart and showing why it didn't hold. Everything else, the ad hominem and the tone policing and the responding-to-a-tone, sat on the ladder between. She'd read it twice, then scrolled the chat and felt the embarrassment of recognizing herself on the lower rungs.

"I'd ask them to name the other person's main point before they answer it," she said. "There's this essay. Paul Graham wrote it, 2008, it's called 'How to Disagree.' Seven levels. Name-calling's at the bottom, and the top is refuting the central point."

Ms. Rowe's eyebrows moved, a millimeter. "Did it work, when you tried it?"

"I pasted it into the chat last night," Annabelle said. "Mason said, quote, we get it, you read." She paused. "But then Walid stopped typing in capitals. So, partial credit."

Ms. Rowe wrote something down. Annabelle couldn't see what, and spent a moment deciding whether caring about it was reasonable or just vanity. Then Ms. Rowe slid a paper across the table. "Last part. Written exercise. Ten minutes. Write me a short message to both volunteers that settles the dispute enough that the event happens. Email tone, not chat tone."

The prompt itself felt like a test of structure, of the difference between writing that arranges its points in order and writing that merely vents them in sequence. Annabelle thought about what her mother called her school emails, "the lawyer voice," and about how Walid said the same tone was cold, and how both of them were partly right, and how she did not know yet how to hold both of those in one paragraph. She wrote a draft. She read it. It opened with "I understand both perspectives," which was true but useless, the kind of sentence that tried to subsume a fight under a blanket instead of sorting it. She crossed it out.

The second draft named Walid's central point first, that the cleanup produced images rather than results, and answered it with the two things she knew: the city crew took the heavy hauling, and the volunteers did the bank trash the crews wouldn't touch. Then it named Mason's point, that repeating the same event made their group small and inward, and admitted it was fair. Then it proposed splitting the day, morning at the river, afternoon at the food bank, and asked for objections by Thursday, phrased so that objections were clearly wanted rather than merely tolerated. When she reread it, she found one line that was really just a dressed-up insult, a soft little piece of sophistry implying that anyone still arguing hadn't read the details, and she cut it, though she mourned it briefly, because it had been a good line.

She handed it over. Ms. Rowe read it without expression, which Annabelle decided was the professional equivalent of a poker face and not a verdict.

"One question," Ms. Rowe said. "Say they reply and Walid calls the whole email fake corporate. What then?"

"Then I ask him which part of the plan is wrong," Annabelle said. "The river, the food bank, or the times. And I don't answer anything else he says until he picks one."

Ms. Rowe looked at her for a second longer than comfortable. "You'll hear from us Friday."

Outside, the phone had stopped buzzing, which felt either like peace or like everyone had moved the war somewhere she couldn't see. Annabelle walked to the bus stop and opened the chat. There were ninety new messages. The last one was from Mason: "fine. but if we do the food bank I'm not carrying the rice AGAIN." She stood under the shelter, thumbs hovering, and typed, "Which rice."

"THE RICE, ANNABELLE."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
The restaurant had run out of the good booths by the time Kevin's party arrived, so they were seated near the kitchen, at a table long enough for eight but holding only five: Kevin, his mother, Conrad, Niko, and Ms. Lin, who had taught him AP English and had come because, she said, someone ought to represent the teachers who hadn't given up on him. The waiters had tied a balloon to his chair. It kept brushing the top of his head, and every time it did, Conrad made a small trumpeting noise, and Kevin's mother laughed harder than the joke deserved.

He had wanted this dinner, had planned it for weeks, and now that it was happening he kept catching himself watching it from somewhere slightly outside, the way you watch a movie you already know the ending of. Tomorrow was the ceremony. His gown hung on the back of his bedroom door at home, pressed by his mother and faintly smelling of the dry cleaner's chemicals, and every time he thought of it he felt a heaviness he couldn't name and didn't want to say out loud, because everyone kept telling him it was the best time of his life.

"I keep feeling like it's a funeral," he said, when the appetizers came. "For, like, a version of me."

"That's bleak," said Niko, who was already stealing a dumpling off Conrad's plate. "It's a graduation, man. You're supposed to be happy."

"I am happy. I'm also not." He looked at Ms. Lin, half expecting her to correct him, to dichotomize his feelings into the ones he was allowed to have and the ones he wasn't, but she only lifted her water glass and waited.

"Both things can be true," his mother said, which was what she always said, and which he usually found comforting and tonight found almost unbearable.

The twist came with the entrées. A waiter appeared carrying a plate Kevin hadn't ordered, a slice of cake with a single candle already lit, and behind him walked the manager of the restaurant, and behind the manager, improbably, walked his father, who had said on the phone in April that he would try to make it and whom Kevin had quietly stopped expecting. His mother's face did something complicated and then smoothed itself over, the way she had learned to do. His father stood at the end of the table with his hands in his pockets and said, "I know I'm late. I mean, for like three years late. But I'm here now."

Kevin stared at the candle, at the little wavering flame, and felt a foreboding so precise it was almost like a forecast: that his father would stay for the cake and then for a month and then vanish again, because his father's presence had always been capricious, arriving and leaving according to weather Kevin could never read. He didn't stand up. He didn't not stand up. He said, "There's room if you pull a chair from the bar," and Niko slid down to make space, and that was all the ceremony that moment got.

"What are you doing after," his father asked him later, somewhere between the cake and the coffee, in the tone of a man trying to catch up on four years in one dinner.

"College. In the fall." Kevin turned his fork over on his plate. "It's weird. Everyone keeps asking what I'm going to do, and all I can think about is what's ending."

"Commencement," Ms. Lin said. She said it lightly, not like a lesson, just tossing the word onto the table the way Niko had tossed the dumpling. "Nobody ever thinks about the word itself."

Kevin frowned at her. "What about it?"

But she had gone back to her coffee, and it was Conrad, of all people, who pulled out his phone, thumbed through it for a minute, and then held it up like he'd caught a fish. "It means beginning. That's why they used it for the ceremony. Because you begin a new status, like being a bachelor or a master." He lowered the phone, looking a little embarrassed at his own sincerity. "So tomorrow is literally named for starting. Not finishing."

Kevin sat with that. He had walked into the word his whole life, every May, on banners over other people's gyms, and had never once opened it. It changed the shape of the thing, or maybe it didn't change anything and only named what had been there: that the heaviness wasn't only loss, that the two feelings he kept trying to divide refused to be divided, that maybe they weren't opposites at all. He looked down the table at his father laughing at something Niko had said, at his mother letting herself laugh too, and he thought about how he could not know yet whether his father being here was a beginning or just an interval, and how he would have to let it be uncertain, and how that was maybe the first real thing he had learned as an almost-college student.

Outside, after, the parking lot had emptied and the balloon had come loose from his chair and drifted up to the restaurant's ceiling, where it hung among the light fixtures like something that had decided to stay. His father was saying he'd be at the ceremony tomorrow, taking a seat in the back. He asked if that was all right. Kevin stood by the car with his gown folded over his arm, the plastic dry cleaner's bag catching the sodium light.

"Sit anywhere you want," Kevin said. "Just be there when they call the name."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Test-driven development, popularized by Kent Beck, follows a 'red, green, refactor' cycle: write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code.
story:
The air conditioner in the computer lab rattled like something with a grudge, and Jake sat in front of a monitor that showed thirty-two compile errors, all of them his. He had started, as he always started, by writing the class: fields first, then constructor, then whatever methods seemed reasonable, and only afterward, when the thing already existed and had opinions of its own, a test file. The test file was where the disagreement began. His Book class refused to cooperate, insisting that title was not visible, and Jake understood the complaint without knowing how to answer it. Somewhere in the last hour, staring at red underlines, he had begun to feel enervated in a way that had less to do with being tired than with having built something he could no longer enter.

Anita dropped her bag on the table beside him and peered at his screen without asking. "You wrote the whole class first," she said, in the tone of someone identifying a spill.

"That's the order," Jake said. "Fields, constructor, methods. Then you test it."

"Alex texted me from camp last night," she said, and pulled out her phone, scrolling while Jake pretended not to wait.

She found it and slid the phone across the desk. The message, timestamped 11:47 p.m., read: "ok so my counselor did this thing where she made us write the TEST first. before anything exists. the class literally doesn't exist yet. you write a test that calls the constructor and getTitle and it FAILS, red. then you write just enough of the class to make it pass, green. then you clean it up, refactor. it's called test-driven development, some guy named Kent Beck popularized it. red green refactor. i thought it was the dumbest thing i've ever heard and then it worked and now i'm annoyed."

Jake read it twice. "That's backwards," he said.

"That's what I said. Then she showed me the Board they made."

Ms. Toussaint, who had been circulating between rows with a laminated seating chart she never looked at, paused at their table. She didn't lean in and she didn't lecture; she only asked, "What does the test say the class should do?"

"It says book.getTitle should return the title I gave the constructor."

"Then the test is your customer," she said, and moved on toward a boy in the back who had somehow inverted his entire monitor display.

Jake deleted nothing, because deleting felt like an admission, but he opened a new file and wrote a test first: construct a Book with the title Slaughterhouse-Five, assert that getTitle returned it. The test failed to compile, since Book did not exist in any form the test could see, and the failure felt different from his other failures. It was a clean red, a red with a direction in it. He wrote a skeleton class, made the field private, exposed only the getter, and ran it again. Green. The suddenness of it unsettled him more than the errors had; he was accustomed to code that resisted, and here was code that simply agreed.

He sat back and tried to hold two ideas at once, which was harder than either of them separately. His old way said you build first and check after, the way a carpenter might measure twice and cut once, and there was something in that worth keeping, a certain respect for the finished thing. The new way said the test comes first, that you describe what you want before you know how to make it, and there was something in that too, something almost like honesty. He could not yet say whether they were opposites or whether one contained the other, whether writing the test first was merely writing the design down in a different grammar. Ms. Toussaint had told them once that a truism of engineering was that requirements exist before solutions whether or not anyone writes them down, and Jake suspected that this red-green-refactor cycle was just a way of forcing yourself to admit it. He did not say any of this aloud. He said, "Anita, what do I do about the second book?"

"Make another test. You want the titles not to bleed into each other."

He wrote it: two Books, two titles, two assertions. He made it pass. Then he looked at his class and found he wanted to rename things, to tidy, and remembered the third word in Alex's message and understood that this, too, was part of the cycle, not an optional vanity but a step with a name. He refactored, and the tests still passed, and he sat very still for a moment because the passing meant something had survived a change, which felt like a small proof of solidity in a week when most things about next year felt evanescent. He had a roommate assignment he hadn't opened. He had a deposit deadline and a commuter form and a mother who kept leaving college brochures on the kitchen counter like postcards from a country he had already agreed to visit.

The bell rang for the passing period and nobody in the lab moved, because Ms. Toussaint had a policy about finishing your compile cycle. Jake stayed in his chair, hands off the keyboard now, looking at the old version of his work still open in the other file, the one that refused to cooperate, with its public fields and its confident, unasked-for methods. He could fix it. He could also leave it as evidence, the way you keep a bad first draft.

Anita was gathering her bag. "Tell Alex his method works," she said, "or don't tell him, he'll be unbearable."

Jake pulled out his phone and started typing, then stopped, then typed anyway: "did it your way. test first, red, green, refactor. you were right and i'm not happy about it. question though. what do you do when you don't know what you want yet?" He read it over, thumb hovering, and Ms. Toussaint's voice came down the row announcing that the lab would be open after school for anyone who wanted the machines.

He pressed send.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Computing a binary search's midpoint as (low + high) / 2 can overflow on very large arrays; writing low + (high - low) / 2 gives the same middle without the overflow.
story:
Kohen's basement smelled like laundry detergent and cold pizza, and the three of them had been there since noon with two laptops and a whiteboard propped against the water heater. The regional programming contest was in nine days. Zoey had the algorithm problem, the one everyone said was a freebie if you knew the trick, and she did not know the trick.

"You search a sorted list," Weston said, spinning a marker between his fingers. "Like a phone book."

"I know what a phone book is," Zoey said. She typed a few lines, deleted them, and typed them again. Her first version walked the array from the front, comparing each element to the target until it found it or ran out of list. It worked. It was slow. On ten numbers it took ten checks, and on ten million it took ten million, which Weston pointed out by holding up his phone stopwatch like a piece of evidence in court.

Mr. Rivera had mentioned binary search once, in the last five minutes of a class that had mostly been about the honor code, and all Zoey remembered was the word "halves." So she tried it. She kept a low index and a high index, found the middle, and compared. Too low, throw away the bottom half. Too high, throw away the top. Weston narrated it in a game-show voice while she worked, guessing aloud each time which half she'd discard next, as if he could prognosticate her decisions better than she could make them. She beat him about half the time, which she found satisfying in a way she didn't say out loud.

"Explain why it's better," Kohen said. He was laconic by nature and spent most sessions lying on the couch with his arms crossed, but he asked the sharpest questions. "If the judges ask."

"Because on sorted data, every comparison eliminates half of what's left," Zoey said. "A linear search eliminates one element per step. A million elements, linear takes up to a million steps. Binary takes about twenty." She wrote the numbers on the whiteboard and stood back from them. Twenty and a million did not look like they belonged to the same problem.

They tested it. Ten elements, found. A thousand, found. A list of names Kohen generated from his uncle's customer files, found. Then Weston downloaded last year's practice dataset, the big one, the one the actual judges had used, with tens of millions of records, and Zoey's program crashed before it printed anything.

For a while nobody spoke. The furnace in the corner clicked on. Weston restarted the program, and it crashed again, in the same place, which at least was consistent. Zoey put her cursor on the line where she computed the midpoint and stared at it. She had written it the obvious way, as (low + high) / 2, and it had passed every test they had, and now it was dead.

Kohen got off the couch. That alone meant something. He leaned over her shoulder, read the line once, and said, "The midpoint."

"What about it?"

"low plus high," he said. "On a dataset that size, that sum can overflow. Try low + (high - low) / 2. Same middle, no overflow."

Zoey looked at the line for a long moment. It was strange to think that two ways of writing the same arithmetic could differ at all, that the obvious version carried a hidden failure that only appeared when the numbers got enormous. She had trusted the small tests, and the small tests had been honest, just not honest about everything. She changed the line, saved, and ran the program against the big dataset. Numbers scrolled up the terminal, stopped, and printed the answer, with a running time that made Weston put his stopwatch down without commentary.

She copied the old line and the new line onto the whiteboard, side by side, and underlined nothing, because she wasn't yet sure which part mattered most or how she'd explain it under pressure. "So if the judges ask why my search works," she said, "I tell them about halving. And if they ask why it didn't crash anyone else's, I tell them this."

"Tell them the basement version," Weston said. "The one where the phone book catches fire."

Zoey capped the marker and set it on the ledge. "Run it again," she said, and reached for the keyboard.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: In his 1975 book Discipline and Punish, Michel Foucault used Bentham's panopticon as a metaphor for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation.
story:
The inventory scanner at Ferro's Market beeped twice for every item David bagged, and the camera above the self-checkout lanes watched him do it, a small black dome with a red pinprick that never blinked. He had worked there since September, three evenings a week, and his job was mostly standing where the screen told him to stand whenever a customer's age had to be verified or a weight didn't match what the machine expected. On Tuesday a man bought a single lemon, and the screen flashed "Assistance Required," and David had to press a button to say the lemon was real. The man laughed, but not kindly. "Machine thinks I'm stealing a lemon," he said, and walked out with his receipt held like a ticket he'd been forced to buy.

David had noticed something else over those months. Whenever Mr. Patel, the owner, checked the weekly reports, the same lanes showed the most "interventions," as the software called them, and it was always the lanes closest to the bus stop, where the customers were mostly from the towers on Milliken Road. He had no way to prove anything. The reports were just numbers, and the numbers were just what the system had flagged, and what the system flagged depended on what it had been trained to notice. Still, when he watched an old woman from the towers stand six minutes waiting for an attendant while a man in a cycling jacket zipped through untouched, he wrote the times down in the back of his chemistry notebook.

That Thursday his civics class was preparing a debate about the monitoring software the school board had bought for classrooms, the kind that let teachers see every student's screen from a dashboard. David had been assigned to argue that it was no different from a teacher walking the rows and glancing over shoulders, a grown-up's ordinary attention, moved to a screen. Genesis thought it was worse, and said so with her usual acerbic precision, the kind that made you feel the cut only afterward. "A teacher's glance forgets," she said. "This thing keeps the tape."

He went to the public library on Saturday because he wanted something better than a feeling to argue with. He had a vague memory of a word from a documentary his mother watched, and he found it in a book by a French philosopher, Michel Foucault, published in 1975 and called Discipline and Punish. In it, Foucault took an old architectural idea, Bentham's panopticon, a prison built so that one watcher in a central tower might see every cell without being seen, and used it as a metaphor for how modern institutions controlled people through the possibility of constant observation. You did not need the guard to be looking. You needed only the possibility that he might be.

Monday at lunch, Jessie spread the debate notes across the table and asked David, point blank, which side he was actually on. He told them about the book, keeping the fact straight: 1975, Discipline and Punish, Bentham's panopticon as a metaphor for modern institutions and control through the possibility of constant observation. "Panopticon," Jessie repeated, writing it down. "Sounds like a dinosaur." Genesis leaned over the page, less sharp now, and said the dome camera at Ferro's was the same thing, and David said no, not exactly, because the camera was real and the watcher was a computer, and a computer didn't get bored or look away, and he wasn't sure yet whether that made the metaphor stronger or whether it broke it.

The debate happened on Wednesday and David lost, technically. The other side read out the school's own privacy policy, which stated that the monitoring was "for student safety," and the judges liked the word safety. Afterward, Mr. Banerjee, who taught the class and had said almost nothing during the argument, caught David in the hallway rearranging the chairs. "You had the harder half of the question," Mr. Banerjee said, and then, before David could decide whether that was consolation, he added, "The lever problem. What do you call it in your math class when you prove a small thing first, to lift the big one?" David said, "A lemma." Mr. Banerjee nodded once and went back to his room.

That night, closing shift, David told Mr. Patel about the lanes near the bus stop, the times in his notebook, the six-minute wait. He had decided to say it plainly, without the word bias, because he didn't want to accuse anyone of anything he couldn't prove. Mr. Patel listened while counting the till, and his face did something complicated, and then he said the vendor had chosen the defaults, not him, and that the system would amortize its cost over four years so they were locked in, but that he could move David's station closer to those lanes and put a mirror up so he could see the line. It wasn't a fix. It was a person standing where the algorithm had left a gap.

David finished the shift by wiping down lane four. Above him the dome camera held its red pinprick steady, and he found himself straightening his posture without deciding to, the way you do when you believe someone might be watching, even when the watcher is only a lens feeding a hard drive nobody reads. On his way out he clocked off at the old terminal by the door, and Mr. Patel called from the office, "David, tomorrow you're on lanes one through four." He pushed through the doors into the cold, the notebook heavy in his jacket pocket, and the parking lot empty except for the bus shelter, where a woman was waiting under the light with two grocery bags between her feet.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Chinese red-envelope gifts avoid amounts containing the number four, because the word for 'four' sounds like the word for 'death'.
story:
The park had been transformed overnight, or so it seemed to Simon, who had walked through it two days earlier and found only geese and an abandoned tennis ball. Now red lanterns hung from the pavilion rafters, folding tables groaned under foil trays of dumplings, and his mother was already three rows deep in a conversation with an aunt he could not name. In his jacket pocket sat two crisp red envelopes, one for each of his young cousins, and in his other pocket sat sixty dollars in twenties that he had withdrawn that morning, the last of his spending money until his campus job started in the fall.

"You look like a man doing math," said Lennox, who had come along because his own family was scattered across two states and because, as he put it, free dumplings have no substitute. Camron trailed behind with a paper cup of tea, blowing on it uselessly in the June warmth.

"I am doing math," Simon said. He had planned forty dollars for the older cousin, Wei, who was eleven and had recently developed opinions about sneakers, and twenty for the younger one. It felt proportionate. It felt fair. He said as much, and Lennox shrugged in the mannerism he used for all questions of money, one shoulder rising and falling as though the topic were physically tiresome.

Near the gift table, where aunts were arranging envelopes in a lacquered box, Simon's youngest cousin was being lectured by her grandmother. The girl had come armed with birthday money and intended to give some of it to Wei, whose birthday had somehow fused with today's celebration in the family's crowded calendar. Simon caught the grandmother's tone before he caught her words, the particular pitch she reserved for children who were about to make a mistake in public.

"She's putting in forty," the girl's brother reported to Simon, gleeful, as he passed with a skewer of grilled chicken. "Forty whole dollars. Grandma's about to lambaste her."

Simon looked at the table. The grandmother had gone obdurate, arms crossed, jaw set, and the girl stood before her with the envelope held in both hands like an offering she did not understand had been rejected. Around them the pavilion was filling, and Simon's mother had already called to him twice about the exchange starting at noon, twenty minutes away, because the elders wanted the gifts given before the lion dancers arrived and everything became chaos.

He approached the table slowly. He knew the grandmother distantly, the way he knew most of the adults here, through childhood photographs and the smell of her cooking. The girl saw him first and turned, holding up the envelope, and he could see the two twenties through the paper's thin fold.

"I saved it all month," she said. "Forty is even. It's a good number."

The grandmother said something to her in Cantonese, sharp and brief, and the girl's face crumpled with the particular injustice of being corrected in a language she was still learning. Simon hesitated, then knelt to the girl's level, because he remembered being corrected like this, years ago, in this same park, by this same woman, over some envelope he had sealed wrong.

He took out his own envelopes and his own bills and laid them on the table where she could see. "I was going to do forty too," he said quietly. "Nobody ever told me either. My mom never explains, she just says do it differently." He looked up at the grandmother, testing, and she gave him a small nod that authorized nothing but did not stop him.

"Four sounds like death," the girl's brother said from behind Simon, matter-of-fact, mouth full of chicken. "That's why Grandma freaked out. Eight is lucky. Six is lucky. Four is like handing somebody bad luck in an envelope."
