The girl looked at her forties, then at Simon's bills, then at her grandmother, who had unfolded her arms and was now smoothing the envelope flat with one thumb. Simon offered the girl a trade, his three twenties for her two, and she counted it out on the table, sixty, her lips moving, before handing the envelope back to her grandmother for approval.

They resealed it together, the girl licking the flap with great ceremony. Somewhere beyond the pavilion, drums began, and Camron appeared at Simon's elbow saying the lion dancers were coming up the hill, and Lennox said they'd better get to the front if they wanted to see anything. Simon pocketed his remaining twenty and his second envelope, the one still addressed to Wei, still empty, still undecided.

"Sixty for Wei, or thirty," he muttered, mostly to himself, as they pushed into the crowd. "Or twenty and save the rest for textbooks."

"Or twenty-eight," Lennox said. "Eight's lucky, apparently. Twice."

The drums grew louder, and the first lion, red and gold, shook its head at the crowd.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Sustained Investigation section asks for 15 digital images and counts for 60 percent of the score.
story:
According to my extremely detailed records, which I had definitely not written on the back of a pizza receipt two minutes ago, I had the whole portfolio figured out. Ten pieces, one theme, done by spring, easy. I am, if anything, a planner. Ask anyone. Actually, don't ask River, because River once watched me do an entire physics lab the morning it was due, but River exaggerates.

The theme had come to me in the kitchen, which is where all my best ideas ferment while my dad's sourdough does the same on the counter above the fridge. Doors. Ten paintings of doors: the screen door at my grandmother's old place, the janitor's closet at school, the little gate in a fence that goes nowhere. I told my dad, and he said it sounded "very liminal," which he'd learned from a podcast, and I said thank you, and I did not ask what it meant. A theme you have to explain is still a theme. Probably.

Taylor came over that Thursday with two energy drinks and a laptop with a cracked screen, and we sat on my bedroom floor to build the plan. Taylor was doing the same portfolio for their school's art program, the local one, the ten-piece one with an artist's statement. "Mine's birds," Taylor said. "Birds doing taxes. Don't laugh." I laughed. "Ten is the number," Taylor said. "Ten pieces, one statement, hand it in, graduate, never draw again."

"Ten," I agreed, and I wrote TEN on the pizza receipt with a flourish, and that's when Taylor's cracked laptop, open to some AP page they'd been scrolling for their cousin, showed me a sentence that rearranged my entire evening. I leaned over and read it again, because I am not always a fast reader under pressure. The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Sustained Investigation section asks for 15 digital images and counts for 60 percent of the score.

"Fifteen," I said.

"Fifteen," Taylor confirmed, sipping an energy drink at 8 p.m. like a person with no regard for their own future.

The thing was, Mr. Yip, my art teacher, had told our class in September that we should consider submitting the AP portfolio alongside the school one, and I had nodded at the time while thinking about lunch. I had filed it under "later," a folder that, in my head, is enormous and beautifully organized. Mr. Yip was now on sabbatical, or furlough, or something, some word the school used that meant he was temporarily not there and couldn't answer my panicked email. I'd sent it anyway. Subject line: "quick question, not an emergency," which was a lie I felt okay about.

I called River, who answers the phone like it's 1997. "River. If I'm building ten pieces for the school portfolio, and the AP Sustained Investigation section asks for fifteen digital images and it's worth sixty percent of the score, what do I do?"

"Draw more doors?" River said. "Also, hi, I'm fine, thanks for asking."

Here is where I'd like to say I blended two brilliant perspectives. What actually happened is I sat on the floor and argued with myself out loud while Taylor ate my emergency crackers. One voice said the theme was the thing, the doors, the idea, and the AP thing was extrinsic, a hoop, a number someone else invented. The other voice said the hoop was the actual game, and besides, five more doors wasn't the hoop diluting the theme; it was the theme getting room to actually do something. Ten doors is a list, maybe. Fifteen doors is a neighborhood. I did not know that for sure, and I said so, out loud, twice, which made Taylor say, "You okay?"

"Uncertain," I said. "Comfortably uncertain. It's a vibe."

Taylor looked at me over the cracker bag. "So it's fifteen images for the AP thing, sixty percent of the score. And ten for school."

"Unless I find out Monday that it's worse than that."

We drew until eleven, Taylor sketching a robin holding a W-2, me doing a fast, ugly pencil version of my grandmother's screen door with the little hook latch, the one that never quite caught and let the wind in all night. It was the best thing I'd made in weeks. Outside my window the streetlight came on, and our neighbor's back gate, the one I could see from the floor, swung open an inch on its own, like it had been waiting for someone to finally notice it.

I took a photo of the sketch with my phone. "Number one," I said. Taylor raised their energy drink.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story 'The Tell-Tale Heart', the narrator insists he is not mad while describing how he murdered an old man.
story:
The bus smelled of diesel and orange peel, and Aaron had thirty-two minutes of it between his driveway and the school, which was exactly long enough to finish the reading if the potholes cooperated. They didn't. He held the paperback against his knee and read the same paragraph four times while the driver braked for a dog that wasn't there.

"You're doing the Poe," Leanna said, dropping into the seat across the aisle. "Ms. Dang assigned it yesterday. Everyone's doing the Poe."

"I'm doing it now," Aaron said. "That's different."

He read it aloud in his head, which was slower but stuck better. The narrator kept stopping to tell him things. You fancy me mad. Madmen know nothing. But you should have seen me. Hear how calmly, how calmly I can tell you the whole story. Aaron looked up at the window, at Francisco's mailbox going by, and thought about a pundit he'd watched with his father the night before, a man on television insisting he had never said the thing there was video of him saying.

Francisco boarded at the next stop and took the seat behind Leanna without asking, because that was his seat, had been his seat since tenth grade. "The eye," he said immediately, as though continuing a conversation they hadn't started. "The vulture eye. That's the whole reason? He kills an old man because of an eye?"

"That's what he says," Aaron said.

"What else would there be?"

It was a reasonable question, and Aaron had no answer, which was its own kind of information. He read on. The narrator was meticulous. He loved the old man. He had nothing against him. He opened the door so quietly, night after night, for seven nights, an hour each night, and on the eighth the old man woke, and the narrator heard something, a low, dull, quick sound, and decided it was the old man's heart. In 1843, Aaron noted, checking the copyright page, Poe had written all this, and the narrator had been insisting the whole time that he was not mad.

"You're smiling," Leanna said.

"I think he's lying."

Francisco leaned between the seats. "About killing the guy? He confesses at the end. He tells the cops where the body is. Chops up the floorboards himself."

"Not about that. About being sane. He says madmen know nothing, and then he proves he knows everything, every detail, every minute, and he thinks that's his defense." Aaron tapped the page. "It's the protests. The minute he says he's not mad, you start counting the ways he might be."

Leanna took the book out of his hand without asking, the way she did, and read a page with her thumb holding her place in her own paperback, which was about a girl and a war and looked more difficult than anything Ms. Dang had ever assigned. "People on the news do this," she said. "Nobody's asking whether they're sane. They just keep saying it."

"They equivocate," Francisco said, pleased with the word, though Aaron wasn't sure he'd used it right, and then wasn't sure he himself would use it right, and let it go.

The bus hit the long hill by the quarry where cell service died, and everyone's phone went quiet at once, which was the only peaceful thirty seconds of the ride. Aaron took the book back and tried to write a margin note. The narrator says he's not mad. That's what makes me doubt him. It felt too simple written down, an inchoate idea that had seemed sharper in his head. Because it wasn't just that the man protested too much. It was that everything Aaron knew about the murder, he knew from the murderer. There was no other witness inside the story. The old man never spoke except to ask who was there. The neighbors heard a shriek and that was all. If you wanted to know what actually happened, you had exactly one source, and that source had opened the bedroom door with a lantern shuttered to a single thread of light and called that caution rather than madness.

"Maybe," Leanna said, watching him not write. "Or maybe he is sane, and it's worse. A sane person who decides an eye is a reason."

Aaron had not considered that, and disliked how much he disliked considering it now, with the school coming up on the right, yellow brick, flagpole, the usual. He had wanted the story to be a machine you could take apart, the way he took apart the toaster last summer, screws in a row on the towel. But the story kept its screws somewhere he couldn't find.

Ms. Dang was on bus duty at the loop, clipboard against her coat, waving them through the doors. "You'll have thoughts tomorrow," she said as Aaron passed, not a question. "About who you believe and why."

He believed the narrator about the lantern, the shutters, the hour. He did not believe him about the heart, and he could not say where the line was between the two, or whether trusting part of a man meant anything at all when the rest of him was a lie. He put the paperback in his bag, zipped it, and followed Francisco up the steps, the doors closing behind them with a sound like a sigh.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Dividing a large batch into shallow containers helps it cool quickly in the fridge, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours.
story:
The assignment on the board said one week of meals, planned, shopped and cooked in batches, all due Friday, and Stella had already spent two evenings failing at the first part. Her first plan eviscerated itself by Wednesday night: three dinners depended on cilantro, which her mother refused to have in the house, and a fourth assumed a slow cooker they did not own. Her second plan was so austere that even she, who liked plain food, could see it belonged to some ascetic in a cave rather than a person with homework and a bus pass: rice, beans, rice, beans. She was still staring at it when Ayoub leaned over from the next station in the cooking classroom and said, "Mine has lasagna on day one and regret on day four. Want to trade problems?"

They did not trade, exactly, but they ended up planning together, which Ms. Demir permitted as long as each of them cooked a separate batch. Ayoub wanted to cook for his grandmother, whose kitchen he had taken over since her hands got bad, and Stella wanted to cook for a reason she did not say out loud: her father worked the late shift now, and someone had to make sure the fridge held more than his energy drinks and her frozen pizzas. Tomas, who was doing the assignment alone because he claimed group work was a scam, kept circling their table to look at their shopping list with open envy. "You have a budget line for losses," he said. "What are losses?" "Onions I ruin," Stella said. "A whole bag of onions, probably."

The shopping trip was its own education. Ms. Demir had given them a price cap and a Wednesday deadline for receipts, and Stella learned that dried lentils cost almost nothing while the pre-cooked ones cost as much as a sandwich, and that buying a whole chicken and cutting it up herself was cheaper than the pieces until she factored in what her mother called the gross factor. In the produce aisle Ayoub held up two sweet potatoes and asked whether they counted as a week's worth of hope or just a week's worth of starch. "Both," Stella said, and put them in the basket, and wrote down the price.

Friday they cooked. The room smelled like garlic and scorched oregano, and Tomas set off the smoke alarm with a tray of chickpeas, and Ms. Demir moved through the stations saying little, only occasionally lifting a lid and asking a question. Stella's big dish was a pot of soup, the largest the classroom had: lentils, the sweet potatoes, a ham hock her mother had contributed as an investment. It had to be refrigerated by the end of the period because it was going home to feed four people across the weekend. She lifted the pot with both towels and set it, whole and steaming, into the fridge space she had claimed.

Ayoub, who was portioning his own sauce beside her, watched her do it and frowned. "At my grandmother's community kitchen, the volunteers would never do that," he said. "They divide a big batch into shallow containers, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours." Stella looked at the pot, at its depth, at the steam still rising off the centre of it, and felt the incipient panic of someone watching a deadline fail quietly from the inside. There was half an hour left in the period. The soup was still near boiling at its core.

She found the stack of takeaway containers at the back shelf, the flat ones, and ladled the soup into six of them, maybe two inches deep each, and slid them onto different shelves with gaps between them so the cold air could move. It was her own idea to spread them out; nobody had told her that part, and she could not have said for certain whether it mattered. Tomas drifted over, still fanning his chickpea tray, and stuck his finger near the surface of one container. "That one's already not hot," he reported, sounding almost friendly about it.

But the problem that she had not solved, and could not solve by Friday, was what she would do next week, when there was no classroom fridge and no stack of shallow containers and no Ayoub at the next station. She had learned to plan and shop, and she had learned this thing about hot food in deep pots, and she had learned that she liked feeding people more than she had expected to like anything practical. What she had not figured out was whether cooking for her father every Sunday was a way of taking care of him or a way of asking him to notice, and she suspected the answer was both, tangled together, and that no assignment would untangle it.

At the bell Ms. Demir checked her containers, marked something on her clipboard, and said, "This one actually thought about cooling. Most of them didn't." Stella carried the six containers to the bus in a canvas bag, the warmth of them fading through the fabric against her hip, and texted her father from the stop: soup when you get home, it's in flat ones, they cool fast. He replied with a single thumbs up, and she stood there a while longer, watching the road for headlights.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people.
story:
The tournament had paused for lunch, and Vincent sat in the empty hallway outside the auditorium with a legal pad on his knees, trying to write a play about the summer his grandmother taught him to make bread. Mr. Navarro had assigned it before they left that morning: a ten-minute play, due in two weeks, drawn from a moment in their own lives. Vincent had assumed the hard part would be remembering. It turned out the hard part was that his play had, so far, a kitchen, a garden, a hospital waiting room, a porch at dusk, a car, and the bakery where his grandmother used to work, plus eleven characters including two cousins he had not seen since he was nine.

"You're writing it here?" Emile dropped down beside him, still in his suit from the quarterfinal, tie loosened. "You're supposed to be recuperating. We lost on a split decision, Vincent. You're allowed to sulk."

"I'm sulking and writing." Vincent turned the pad so Emile could see the crossed-out list of locations. "It doesn't fit. It's like a whole summer and I've got ten minutes."

Emile tilted his head, which was his way of thinking. "Trenton did one of these last year. The drama teacher made him cut everything down. One room, like three people." He shrugged. "You should ask him, but that's what he said."

Vincent found Trenton in the cafeteria line, holding a plate with nothing on it yet, staring at the options with the concentration of someone ranking contentions. Trenton was taciturn on his best days, but when Vincent described the six locations and the eleven relatives, Trenton actually put his plate down.

"Yeah, no," Trenton said. "A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters. There's no time to change scenery or introduce a bunch of people. That's just how it is." He picked the plate back up and moved toward the pasta.

Vincent stood there holding his legal pad, feeling the sentence rearrange everything. One setting. Few characters. He walked back down the hallway, past rooms where debaters were prepping, and heard his own habits in a new light: in debate he had been trained to cover everything, to win the whole resolution, to summarize a year of policy evidence in four minutes. He had been writing the play the way he wrote a case. But ten minutes was not a case. Ten minutes was one room held still long enough to see into it.

He chose the kitchen. Not the hospital, not the bakery, not the porch where everyone had gathered afterward. The kitchen, on a morning when his grandmother's hands were shaking too much to knead and she talked him through it anyway, flour on the counter, the radio on, no one else home. He crossed out the cousins. He crossed out the waiting room. He kept her, and he kept a phone call from his mother that came in the middle and that his grandmother refused to answer, which was the truest thing he knew about that day and had never once said out loud.

Between rounds, he read a draft of the first scene aloud to Emile in the stairwell. Emile listened with his eyes closed, which he did when he was being fair to something. "The part where she won't pick up the phone," he said afterward. "That's it. That's the play." He paused. "You should finish it here, honestly. You're different at tournaments. Faster, or something."

Mr. Navarro found them there, coffee in hand, and asked how the assignment was going. Vincent told him about the six locations, a little ashamed of them now, the way one is ashamed of an early draft even when it was a necessary one. But Mr. Navarro only nodded. "So you found the shape of it," he said. "Most students fight that for a week." He did not say more, which Vincent was grateful for, and moved on to check on the team from the other school.

Vincent worked through the afternoon rounds with the pad folded into his jacket, and between cross-examinations he added lines: her voice, which was lower than people expected, her habit of naming the dough as if it were a person, the way she said "let it rest" and meant two things. He was not sure yet whether the ending should be the bread coming out of the oven or the phone ringing a second time, unanswered again. One was an image and one was a wound, and he could not decide if a play was allowed to be both.

On the bus home, Emile slept against the window and Trenton sat across from Vincent, watching him write. When Vincent finally set the pen down, Trenton leaned over and read the last page without asking, which was how Trenton did most things. He was quiet for a long moment. Then he said, "You should submit it. To the spring thing. The one where they stage them."

"You think it's ready?"

Trenton looked out the window at the highway lights coming on, one after another. "It's not," he said. "Do it anyway."

Vincent turned back to the page, to the stage direction he had left half-finished: The oven timer goes off. She does not move. Vincent picks up the pad, crosses out his next line, and writes her answer instead.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
The house still smelled of lavender and the noxious ghost of mothballs, and Megan stood in the hallway holding a trash bag, not sure whether she was allowed to throw anything away yet. Her grandmother had died eleven days ago, on a Tuesday, between a load of laundry and a phone call Megan's mother never got to finish. The family had come to the house now to sort it, and Megan had been assigned the linen closet, which meant she was supposed to be folding towels while everyone else cried in the kitchen.

She hadn't cried yet. That was the problem she kept circling back to, the way you touch a bruise to see if it still hurts. At the funeral she had held Jorge's hand and felt mostly an itch in her tights. She had laughed at the reception when Baby did an impression of the pastor's cough, and then felt like a criminal, as though laughing might exculpate her from loving anyone. She kept waiting for the sadness to arrive on schedule, the way the pamphlet in the funeral home lobby had implied it would, with its tidy staircase of stages.

Jorge showed up around noon, because Jorge always showed up, carrying two sandwiches and his phone. "I have to tell you something," he said, sitting on the bathtub edge while Megan folded. "I keep going to school. I keep, like, laughing at Mr. Klein's jokes. And at the viewing I was fine for two hours. Is that wrong? My aunt says I'm in denial and the anger is coming."

Megan sat down on the bath mat. She had been wondering the same thing about herself for eleven days, and hearing it out loud made the question feel suddenly public, a thing with edges. "Hold on," she said, and pulled out her own phone, because last week, unable to sleep, she had typed into a search bar, is it normal not to cry when someone dies, and had scrolled past the forums until she found a study she'd screenshot but never read carefully.

She read it aloud, slowly, the way she read exam questions. A psychologist named George Bonanno had studied bereaved people, and what he found was that resilience was common. Not rare, not suspicious. Common. And there were no mandatory stages that everyone had to pass through after a loss. No staircase. No schedule. She read the sentence twice, and the second time something in her chest loosened like a knot in a shoelace.

"So we're not doing it wrong," Jorge said. "There's no wrong."

"There's no one right way, anyway." Megan was careful about that distinction, careful not to turn a study into a rule, which would be its own kind of pedantry. She knew that finding out you were normal wasn't the same as being finished. She still didn't know why the towels made her throat tighten when the funeral hadn't, why folding a stack her grandmother's hands had bleached soft did what the casket could not. Maybe grief just kept its own appointments. She was honest with herself about that part: the study told her she wasn't broken, but it couldn't tell her when, or whether, the crying would come.

The two of them worked through the linen closet together. Baby arrived at two with her bike helmet still on, and by four the three of them had filled six bags and found a tin of shortbread hidden behind the good tablecloth, still sealed. Megan pried it open, and the smell rose up lavender-sweet, and it was like her grandmother had leaned in close to say something. Her eyes burned, then spilled, quick and quiet, and she let them, and she also kept chewing, and both of those things were true at once.

Jorge put his hand briefly on her shoulder. Baby took off her helmet, finally, and set it on the sink like an offering.

"Okay," Megan said. She wiped her face with the corner of a towel her grandmother would have said was too good for that, folded the rest of the stack, and put the tin in her backpack, wrapped in the good tablecloth, to take home.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, a new employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck.
story:
Rachel had circled the coffee shop three times before she made herself go in, reading the small card taped to the register window the way you might read a dare. HELP WANTED, WEEKENDS, ASK FOR MANAGER. Inside, the air smelled of scorched milk and something sweeter underneath, and a man behind the counter was wiping the espresso machine with a cloth that had seen better decades.

"You're Rachel," he said before she spoke. "You sit by the window. Medium drip, no room." He introduced himself as Mr. Nakamura, the owner, and set the cloth down. "You applied Tuesday. You wrote that you were, quote, dependable and curious." He looked at her over his glasses. "Dependable is a habit. Curious I can't teach. Which do you want to be?"

She said both, and he hired her on the spot, which produced in her a flash of exhilaration so sudden she nearly laughed at the wrongness of timing. He slid a folder across the counter, told her the paperwork could be done before her shift started Saturday, and went back to the machine.

The paperwork was where things stopped being simple. At home that night she opened the folder on her bed and found a form she had never seen, dense with boxes and instructions, and the words on it seemed to belong to a country she was supposed to already be a citizen of. She texted a photo of it to her mother, who replied from the night shift with a shrug in the form of a single question mark. She texted Khaled, whose reply was immediate and useless: idk, that's taxes, that's adult stuff, good luck soldier. She sat with the form for a long moment, chewing the end of a pen, and then she did what curiosity had always made her do. She read it.

It took longer than it should have, and she went down a small rabbit hole doing it, because the form was not just a form, it was a question the government was asking her, or rather asking her employer about her. As far as she could work out, a new employee filled out Form W-4 so the employer knew how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. Withhold. She said the word out loud to her empty room and found she liked it, the way it meant money taken now so it wouldn't be owed later, a whole theory of patience embedded in a single verb. She filled in the boxes slowly, and when she finished she still wasn't certain she'd done it right, only certain that she understood what the form was for, which felt like a different and possibly more important kind of right.

Saturday she arrived early, folder under her arm, and Mr. Nakamura checked her form with the air of a man grading a quiz he expected everyone to fail. He grunted. "Most kids have their parents fill this out," he said. "Yours has your handwriting all over it. Your crooked handwriting."

"You can tell that from the boxes?"

"I can tell a person who reads instructions from a person who doesn't." He filed the form away and handed her an apron. Then, over the first hour, the morning rearranged everything she'd prepared for. It was not the register that defeated her, though the register tried, and it was not the noxious smell of the cleaning chemical she had to swab the milk wand with, which stung her nose and made her eyes water. It was Brandon, who walked in at nine wearing the same green apron she was wearing. Brandon, who had been working there for three weeks and had never mentioned it once at school, and who now stood at the grinder beside her saying, "Wait, you got hired too?" in a voice that suggested she had wandered into a private club.

They didn't speak much for the first hour, both of them concentrating, both of them aware of the other concentrating. When the morning rush thinned, Brandon loaded a portafilter and said, without looking at her, "I didn't tell people because I didn't want everyone asking me for free coffee." She said that was fair. He asked how much she was making, she told him, and it was more than he was making, and they both stood there letting that fact sit between them like a third person in the small space behind the counter. She thought about asking Mr. Nakamura why, and didn't yet, and thought she probably would on Monday, and thought about how to phrase it so it didn't sound like either an accusation or a surrender. Brandon tamped the grounds down hard, twice.

"So," he said finally, pulling a shot that came out pale and wrong, "you want to learn the grinder, or the register first?"

Rachel looked at the line of cups above the machine, the steam curling off the drip brewers, the little brass shelf where the tips went. "Both," she said. "But start with the grinder."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index.
story:
Nathan had written the same sentence four times, and each version was worse. His economics essay was due Monday, and the assignment seemed simple at first: explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. He could do that part. Raise the cost of borrowing, people buy less, prices stop climbing so fast. What he could not do was the last paragraph, the one Ms. González had underlined twice on the rubric: "So what? What should inflation actually be?" She had written "2 percent?" beside it with a question mark, and Nathan had stared at that question mark until it seemed to presage his entire grade collapsing.

He was still staring when Finlay dropped into the chair across from him in the library and slid a granola bar across the table like a bribe. Finlay wanted something; Nathan could tell from the angle of his shoulders, which were set in the particular posture of a person about to ask for a favor.

"Don't say it," Nathan said.

"Debate team," Finlay said anyway. "Regionals are in three weeks and we lost Marcus to the robotics trip. I need a second speaker. You're good at arguing. You argue with me constantly, free of charge."

"I don't argue. I correct you. There's a difference."

"That's literally arguing."

Nathan rubbed his eyes. "I have an essay I can't finish. I can't figure out why two percent inflation counts as success. Why not zero? Zero seems like the obvious goal. Prices stay the same. Done."

Finlay peeled the granola bar slowly, thinking, which was something he did more often than people gave him credit for. "Okay, but here's a thought. Is two percent even a real thing, or is it just what economists say? Like, did somebody official actually decide it, or is it folklore?"

That was the question Nathan had been circling without naming. He opened his laptop and typed in a search, half expecting a wall of hedging, the kind of answer that meant nobody really knew. Instead he found something crisp. He read it twice, then a third time, because it was so plain it felt like a trick.

"On January 25, 2012," he said, reading aloud, "the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index."

"The what index?"

"Personal consumption expenditures. PCE." Nathan leaned back. "It's an actual date. It's not folklore. Before 2012 they didn't have an explicit number at all, and then one day in January they just said it. Two percent, that's the target, that's what success looks like."

Finlay chewed for a while. "So your paragraph isn't really about why two is the right number. It's about the fact that someone finally committed to a number. Like, the interesting part is the committing."

Nathan looked at his draft, at the four dead sentences, and felt something shift. He had been trying to derive two percent from first principles, as if it were a lemma in a geometry proof, one truth that followed necessarily from another. But maybe it wasn't like that at all. Maybe it was a decision, made by people, on a date, with a specific measuring stick attached, and the honesty of his essay lay in saying so. The mechanism he understood, the raising of rates and the slowing of demand, that was the machine. The target was the hand on the dial. Two different kinds of thinking, and he had been smashing them together like they were one thing.

Adrianna appeared at the table with her own laptop and no explanation, which was her way. She had a free period and a habit of adopting other people's problems. When Nathan explained the date, the index, the target, she frowned at her screen.

"Wait, so for years before that, everyone was fighting inflation without agreeing on what winning meant?" she said. "That's like the soccer team practicing all season and never deciding what the score should be."

"Basically."

"That's insane. That's also your essay. That's your so-what paragraph, Nathan, write it before you lose it."

He wrote it. The paragraph came out fast and then he slowed down, because the last sentence mattered. He typed that the Fed had made its commitment explicit in 2012, naming the number and the index, and that whether two percent was the right number was a separate question from whether a central bank should name a number at all. He sat with that sentence. It felt true and it felt unfinished, and he decided the unfinished part was the honest part. Ms. González had once told the class that a good economics paper ends where the thinking actually ends, not where the thinking would be convenient to end. He hoped she meant it.

Ms. González kept him after class on Tuesday. She had his essay in her hand, folded once, and she tapped the final paragraph with two fingers. "This is the part I couldn't get out of you last unit," she said. "You used to write like the answer was somewhere in the textbook, waiting. This time you wrote like someone who found a real fact and then sat with what it didn't tell you."

"Is that a good thing or a bad thing?"

"It's the whole thing." She handed the paper back, and he saw the grade, and it was better than he expected, though not perfect, which somehow made it feel more real.

At lunch, Finlay slid into the seat across from him and put a debate team sign-up sheet on Nathan's tray, already filled out except for one line.

"No," Nathan said.

"You owe me. I asked you the question that fixed your essay."

"You asked me if it was folklore. That's not a contribution, that's a personality." But he was already reading the sheet, and the topic for regionals was printed at the top: monetary policy, resolved, that central banks should set explicit targets. The room got very slightly louder around him. Somewhere near the windows, a teacher was wheeling a cart of metamorphic rock samples, leftovers from the geology unit, each one a record of pressure and slow change.

Nathan picked up the pen. "One condition," he said. "I get the opening speech, and you have to let me say the date."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The stage manager records the blocking in the prompt book so that it can be repeated the same way at every performance.
story:
Andrew had signed the form in September mostly because Ms. Schneider had said the drama program needed a student director this year, and because he liked the idea of being the one who decided things. By the second week of October he understood that deciding things was mostly standing in the middle of the school auditorium saying the word "again."

"Elaina, when you say the line about the river, you cross downstage left. Past the chair."

"I did cross."

"You drifted. There's a difference between crossing and drifting."

Magnus, sprawled in the third row of seats with his script open on his knees, gave his laconic verdict. "She drifted."

Elaina threw a rolled-up sock at him, which was the level of discourse in the second week. The one-act was twenty-two minutes long and had four actors, and Andrew had spent a full Sunday taping the floor of the stage with spike marks, small silver X's that the light caught whenever anyone moved. He had drawn diagrams in a fat black binder, arrows and stick figures, positions numbered like chess moves. He called it his bible, mostly to himself.

The trouble was that blocking, he discovered, was not the same as knowing blocking. He could put the actors where he wanted them. He could not yet make the reason for the placement survive contact with the actors themselves. When Elaina crossed on the river line it looked mechanical, an extruded motion with nothing inside it, a shape pushed out of a machine. He tried to explain the feeling of it and failed, and she stood on her silver X looking at him with her chin up, waiting.

"I don't know," he finally said. "Just try it as if you're leaving and you can't."

She tried it that way, and it worked, and neither of them said anything about it, which he understood was its own kind of courtesy.

Ms. Schneider came to a run-through in the last week and sat in the back with her coat still on. Afterward she asked him one question, which was who kept his prompt book when he wasn't there. He said he did, obviously. She looked at him for a moment and then said goodnight, and he spent the walk home being annoyed and then less annoyed and then awake at midnight, because the stage manager, a quiet senior whose name always escaped him at the wrong times, had been sitting in the wings every rehearsal with a binder of her own.

He found her the next day in the cafeteria and asked what was in it. She showed him: his blocking, all of it, recorded move by move in a shorthand of arrows and abbreviations, so that it could be repeated the same way at every performance. He had been walking around with the plan in his head. She had been walking around with the plan on paper, and paper didn't get tired or second-guess itself at eleven at night.

"You've been writing down everything I said?"

"Everything that happened," she said. "You said some of it."

On opening night the auditorium was fuller than he had expected, forty or fifty people, his mother in the second row pretending not to be his mother. The play went well until it didn't. In the third scene, Elaina's scene partner, a boy who had never once forgotten a cross in rehearsal, dried completely, standing center stage like a fence post, and Elaina improvised a line to cover it, and the boy moved the wrong direction, cutting her off from the chair, and the whole geometry of the scene began to collapse.

In the wings afterward, between scenes, the boy insisted he had gone the right way. "I cross right there. I've always gone right."

Elaina said he had always gone left, and it got louder, and the stage manager appeared between them with her binder already open, and put her finger on the page. "Scene three, the cross is left," she said, and that was the end of the argument, because the book was the book. Andrew stood a little apart and watched his own arrows settle it, lines he had drawn weeks ago reaching through the paper and fixing a room he couldn't otherwise touch.

The final scene went clean. When the lights came down the applause was ordinary and real, and afterward Elaina found him in the lobby, still half in costume.

"The drifting was better tonight," she said. "Don't let it go to your head."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: The Common European Framework of Reference describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options.
story:
The printout of the course outline had been folded twice in Audrey's backpack since June, and now, in the front room of her grandmother's house, she smoothed it open on the table beside the fruit bowl. Somewhere in the list of objectives, between "narrate past events" and "write a formal letter," she found the sentence she had half remembered on the train: the Common European Framework of Reference describes a B2 speaker as able to explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. She read it twice. The exam in September wanted five minutes of argument, entirely in French, and the outline did not say she had to win. It said she had to weigh.

The house smelled of dish soap and warm cherries from the bowl, and the afternoon had gone torpid, the curtains hanging without moving, a fly ticking against the window glass. Her grandmother was out back picking the last of the currants, and Audrey had the room to herself, which was the point of coming here: two weeks at the end of summer, a grandmother who spoke almost no English, and a deadline.

She had chosen her topic back in the spring, when it had seemed abstract, the way school topics do. Should cities make public transit free for everyone under twenty-five? At the time it had been a convenient question, rich in vocabulary she already knew. Now, sitting in a village where the bus came twice a day and everyone on it was over sixty, the question had grown feet. Her grandmother rode that bus to the market on Thursdays. Free fares were aimed at people like Audrey, not people like her grandmother, and Audrey had written her draft as though the bus existed only for students.

She opened her notebook and read her opening paragraph aloud, quietly, in French. It came out stiff. Every sentence had the same architecture, subject then verb then object, like a fence. She could hear the syntax straining under what she wanted to say, and what she wanted to say had changed since she had written it.

Ember arrived on bicycle at four, sweating, carrying a bag of cherries she had clearly stolen from her own garden, since they were the same cherries. Ember was doing the same exam, on a different topic, and they had agreed, by text, to practice together. Ember dropped into the chair opposite and said, in English, "So are we arguing or are we thinking."

"Both," Audrey said. "That's the problem. My draft argues like a lawyer. It litigates the other side instead of considering it." She turned the notebook so Ember could see. "I found the level descriptor for the exam. B2. Listen to this." She read the sentence from the outline aloud, slowly, so the weight of it landed. "It doesn't say convince. It says explain a viewpoint, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options."

Emner wrinkled her nose. "So we don't have to win."

"We have to be fair." Audrey said it in French, to test it, and found she had no word for fair that she trusted. She tried "juste," then "équilibré," then wrote both in the margin and left them there, unresolved, which felt honest.

They drilled for an hour, Ember counting minutes on her phone, Audrey speaking with her hands because the words came slower than the thoughts. At some point Audrey scrapped her second paragraph entirely and started over, arguing first for the fares, then against, letting the two sides actually touch. The bus her grandmother rode was nearly empty and would stay nearly empty with or without free fares for the young. Free transit would fill the buses in cities, and empty the farebox here, and maybe that was fine, and maybe it wasn't, and Audrey discovered she could hold both of those at once in French, if she spoke slowly enough. Her grandmother came in with the currants near the end, listened from the doorway without understanding the topic, and said Audrey's accent had improved since last summer, which was the kindest lie anyone had told her all year.

Toward six, Ember went to fill their water glasses and Mr. Bélanger from next door appeared at the open window, as he did, holding pruning shears and a remark. He asked, in French, what the two girls were studying so seriously, and Audrey explained, haltingly, the exam, the five minutes, the descriptor she had read. He considered this while chewing the stem of nothing, then said that in his day they had only learned to recite, and that weighing was harder than reciting, and that she should eat more, she was too thin, which was not relevant but which she accepted as encouragement.

After Ember left, Audrey sat with the notebook as the light went long and yellow across the table. She read her new draft through once, in French, and then once more in her head in English, checking that the person arguing was still her. Her position had softened into something less like a banner and more like a held object, turned in the hand: free fares for the young, probably, in cities; out here, the money might matter more than the principle, and she did not yet know where the line between cities and villages actually fell, and she suspected no one did. She circled the sentence about the empty bus and wrote beside it, in French, a question she could not yet answer. Then she closed the notebook, took the last cherry from the bowl, and went out to help her grandmother carry in the currants before dark.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 74 degrees Celsius (165 degrees Fahrenheit).
story:
Alexandre counted the bills in his wallet twice, which changed nothing, and then walked the length of the farmers' market as though he were a connoisseur of vegetables rather than a boy about to start college in an apartment with a stove he had never lit. He had decided, over the summer, in the margins of a brochure about meal planning that his mother had left on his desk without comment, that he would learn to cook in batches: one afternoon of labor, seven days of food, no more forty-dollar delivery orders arriving at eleven at night. The arithmetic appealed to him. He was less sure about the rest of it.

At the tomato stall a man in a canvas apron, whose sign read KOVALENKO, weighed out two kilograms of romas without small talk. When Alexandre asked whether they would keep, the man said, "Roma. Roast them Sunday, they'll be fine." It was the longest sentence anyone had offered him all morning, and it was enough.

He found Alanna near the bread table, arguing gently with a toddler over the last olive loaf. She was starting at the same college and had been cooking for herself since she was fifteen, a fact she mentioned the way other people mentioned their star signs. She inspected his canvas bag, the potatoes, the eggs, the sad bunch of cilantro he had bought because it was near the door. "You're going to cook all of this on Sunday," she said. "Rice, lentils, roasted tomatoes. Containers. You did plan this."

"I planned it," Alexandre said, though the plan existed mostly as a note on his phone that said RICE? and LENTILS? and a third item he had typed while distracted and could no longer interpret.

Yaseen appeared from behind the honey vendor with a jar in each hand, weighing one against the other like a jeweler. He was living in the same building, had already ruined one pot of rice that week, and had opinions. "The trick," he said, "is a thermometer. My sister left hers in my box when she moved out. I'll lend it to you if you let me eat some of whatever this is." He gestured at Alexandre's bag as though it contained a rumor.

On Sunday the apartment smelled like the inside of the market, all afternoon, and by evening Alexandre had seven containers lined up on the counter with days written on masking tape, which he understood was the whole point, the system that kept a week from becoming a series of profligate decisions made while hungry. He texted Alanna a photograph. She texted back a single thumbs up, which felt like a diploma. Then Yaseen arrived with the thermometer, still in its plastic sleeve, and a folded sheet of paper that had been inside the sleeve.

The paper was an insert, mostly warnings about batteries, but near the bottom there was a line that neither of them had expected. Yaseen read it aloud, slowly, holding it at arm's length: "The USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit." Below that, in smaller type, it said 74 degrees Celsius, as though the thermometer were hedging.

"I have never once checked a temperature in my life," Alexandre said. He had assumed that reheating was a matter of steam and impatience, that food went from cold to safe by feel, the way his mother had done it, sliding containers into the microwave with the certainty of long practice. But his mother had forty years of intuition and he had a Tuesday ahead of him and a container of rice that had spent three nights in a refrigerator shared with Yaseen's unlabeled experiments.

He set a pan on the stove, spooned the rice in, and when it steamed he pushed the thermometer's probe into the middle and watched the number climb. It stopped at 140. Yaseen leaned over his shoulder. "That's not 165," he said. "The paper was very clear." Alexandre stirred the rice, waited, pushed the probe in again, a different spot this time, because he had begun to suspect that rice was not uniform, that a single reading was a kind of lie a careful person told himself. The display ticked up, paused, and settled. He angled it so Yaseen could see.

"Seventy-four," Yaseen read off the Celsius side, and then, pointing at the other number, "a hundred and sixty-five. Okay. So it's done." He was already reaching past Alexandre for a fork and the container marked Tuesday, and Alexandre, watching him, did not take it away.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: In a definite integral the constant of integration cancels out, because it is added to both F(b) and F(a) and then subtracted away.
story:
Nicholas arrived at math club with the test folded into his pocket like evidence, and he waited through the announcements before he could stand at the whiteboard and show anyone. Mr. Islam had begun the meeting with a small ritual the club seemed to enjoy, a moment where they lionized a former member now doing graduate work in Zurich, and then he opened the floor. Nicholas uncapped a marker. He wrote the integral from minus one to two of x squared, and beside it his own answer, x cubed over three plus C, evaluated, and then the mark in red pen beside it: minus two, and the word "why?" in the margin where he had written plus C.

"Mr. Islam took off points," he said. "Not for the antiderivative. For the C. On a definite integral." He turned to the room, which was six folding chairs and a supply closet smell and rain ticking against the windows. "So either he's wrong or I'm missing something, and I want to know which."

Caleigh had her feet up on the chair in front of her, which she did when she was thinking and also when she was not. "You put C on everything. You put C on the quiz, on the homework, probably on your name tag at the regional." Ayanna laughed without looking up from her notebook, where she was shading a parabola with the side of her pencil until it looked like a hillside at dusk.

Nicholas wrote the Fundamental Theorem the way he had copied it from the board that afternoon, F of b minus F of a. "Okay. Watch. If the antiderivative is x cubed over three plus C, then F of b is eight thirds plus C." He wrote it. "And F of a is negative one third plus C." He wrote that too, and stepped back, because the next move was the one he had rehearsed on the walk over and he wanted them to see it arrive rather than be told.

Ayanna had stopped shading. From her seat near the window she could see the whole board, the two expressions stacked, the little plus C sitting in each of them like a pebble in two shoes. She watched Nicholas draw the long horizontal line of subtraction, the way he did it slowly, as if the line itself were part of the argument. When he subtracted, the two constants came away together, and what remained was eight thirds plus one third, which was three. She had known the answer was three; the calculator had told her that much an hour ago, when Caleigh texted her a photo of the test. What she had not known was where the C went, and there it was, gone, not because someone erased it but because it had been on both sides of the subtraction and had nowhere left to stand.

"In a definite integral the constant cancels," Nicholas said. "It's added to both F of b and F of a, so when you subtract, it just goes." He tapped the board twice. "It doesn't matter what C is. It could be anything. It subtracts away."

"Then why do we write it at all?" Caleigh asked, and Ayanna recognized the tone, the one Caleigh used when she had already found the answer and was testing whether anyone else could get there. "On the indefinite ones."

"Because there it's the only one," Ayanna said, surprising herself by saying it out loud. "There you're not subtracting anything. There's no second value to cancel it against." She wished immediately that she had put it differently, less like a circumlocution, more like Nicholas with his clean horizontal lines, but nobody seemed to mind. Mr. Islam, who had been listening from the doorway with his arms crossed and a coffee going cold in his hand, nodded once and did not say anything, which in his classroom was its own kind of applause.

They ran the problem again with a different function, then a third, Caleigh calling out antiderivatives while Nicholas wrote, the interval from zero to one, then from two to five, the constants appearing and vanishing in pairs each time like birds leaving a wire from both ends at once. The rain kept up its interminable ticking. Nicholas set the marker down finally and looked at the board, at all that cancelled arithmetic, and wondered whether there was anything else in mathematics that worked this way, something true not because it was simple but because it appeared twice and got out of its own way.

"Next time," Ayanna said, closing her notebook, "you should get marks back. Tell him you can prove it now."

Nicholas folded the test along its old crease. "He wrote why," he said, holding it up to the light. "I'm going to write because it's in both of them, and it subtracts. Right under the red pen."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: At a local maximum of a polynomial the derivative equals zero, because the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal.
story:
Mathis had been sent to his grandfather's house for the week with two suitcases: one of clothes, one of calculus homework. His mother had a conference, his grandfather had a bad hip and a large garden, and the arrangement, according to her, would be "good for everyone," a phrase Mathis had learned to pathologize, since it usually meant something was about to become his responsibility. In this case the something was the garden, and also the shed, and also a metal table covered in jars of his grandfather's cherry preserves, which the old man sold at the Saturday market with an air of mild surprise that anyone wanted them.

"You're doing the maths," his grandfather said on the second evening, not a question. He was a laconic man who communicated mostly through sandwiches and raised eyebrows, and he set a plate down beside Mathis's notebook with the gravity of a diplomat delivering a treaty.

"Derivatives," Mathis said. "And, uh, maxima." He turned the notebook so the old man could see the page, which was mostly arrows.

His grandfather looked at it for a long moment. "The preserves," he said. "I raise the price, fewer people buy. I lower it, more buy but I earn less per jar. Somewhere in between is the best price." He tapped the notebook. "That is your maximum. Find it for me and I'll pay you in preserves."

"Grandpa, that's a whole word problem. I can't just invent data."

The old man shrugged, which in his language meant the conversation was over, and went to bed.

Mathis texted Madilyn at eleven. HELP. My grandfather has turned my homework into a jam cartel. She replied with a voice note in which Gibson, apparently already in the room, could be heard saying, "Jam cartel, that's the band name." Then a longer message from Madilyn, which Mathis read twice under the covers with the flashlight his grandfather kept for power cuts, because the man distrusted bedside lamps on principle: "Okay so think of your profit curve. When you sketch it, the highest point, the top of the peak. At a local maximum of a polynomial the derivative equals zero, because the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal. Flat. Nothing climbing, nothing falling. That's the whole trick, basically. Also Gibson says he wants a jar."

He lay in the dark feeling a faint foreboding, not about the maths but about how simple Madilyn made it sound, as though the thing that had been looming over him all semester could be dismantled by one text. In the morning he tested it. He made up numbers, plausible ones, cherries and sugar and market stall fees, wrote a polynomial for profit against price, and took its derivative, pen moving fast enough to tear the paper once. Then he set the derivative to zero, solved, and got a price. He sketched the curve and there it was, the peak, and the peak was exactly where the flat spot said it would be. He checked it twice, then a third time, and then sat very still on the garden bench while a wasp investigated his ankle.

"So?" his grandfather said at lunch, sandwich, eyebrow.

"Three euros a jar," Mathis said. "Give or take."

The old man chewed for a while. "I charge four."

"Well, four isn't the maximum. I did the maths."

"I've been selling for thirty years, boy."

Mathis felt the two positions collide somewhere in his chest: the curve on one side, neat and provable, and thirty years of Saturdays on the other, which were not nothing. "You could try three for one week," he said. "As an experiment. That's how it works, you have to check." He was honest enough, at least with himself, to admit that the numbers assumed people behaved like numbers, which they famously did not.

His grandfather took a jar from the shelf, dusted it with his sleeve, and set it beside Mathis's notebook. "For Gibson," he said. "Tell him the band name is acceptable." Then he took the notebook, held it at arm's length, and read the page of arrows and torn paper for a long, silent minute.

"Saturday," he said finally, and carried the notebook inside.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
Christopher had ironed the shirt twice, which was once more than the shirt required, and now it hung on his closet door like evidence of something he could not yet name. Chayse sat on the bed watching him, thumbs working the dead screen of an old phone.

"You're going to burn a hole in it," Chayse said. "Third pass and it starts to smoke. That's physics."

"It's one pass. The first one didn't count. The iron wasn't hot."

"Everything's not counting with you tonight." Chayse kicked a sneaker against the bedframe. "Who even cooks for a first date anymore? You take them somewhere with menus. Somewhere with a waiter who can be blamed."

Christopher looked at the kitchen through his doorway. The table was set with his mother's good cloth, the one she kept for holidays, and two plates he had washed twice. He had invited Nadia here because she had said, casually, that restaurants made her feel like she was performing, and he had understood that immediately, the way you understand someone describing a room you have also been locked in. Cooking was something he could actually do. It was the only thing tonight he felt certain of.

"She knows where the exits are," he said. "It's my house, so she knows. That's the whole point."

Ms. Joshi from next door arrived at six with a lemon, because she had heard, through the open window, that he was making the fish and had opinions about the fish. She pressed the lemon into his hands at the door and stayed exactly as long as it took to say that his mother had raised him to be decent, which was a heavy thing to put on a lemon and walk away with.

Nadia came at seven wearing a jacket over her dress because the evening had turned cool, and she stood in the doorway for a second looking at the candles he had lit and then unlit and then lit again, and she said, "You actually cooked," as though she had bet someone he wouldn't. Dinner went better than he had rehearsed it. She told him about her brother, who had taken a gap year and worked what he called a sinecure at their uncle's shop, sitting in the back reading while the register rang itself, and Christopher laughed harder than the joke deserved because relief makes everything funnier. They cleared the plates together and argued gently about whether the neighborhood where they'd grown up was becoming somewhere else, whether the new cafe on the corner was a good thing or a wound, and Nadia said the men who used to sleep in the doorway of the old bank had simply moved three blocks east, that calling a place improved while the indigent among them were merely relocated was a kind of lie people told themselves to assuage something. Christopher said he had never thought of it that way and meant it, and the conversation kept going until it was ten and she said her mother would start texting.

They stood on the porch while he walked her to the car, and somewhere between the door and the steps she took his hand, and his whole mind went quiet and then very loud. He had read enough, in the long unstructured afternoons of the last year, to know the shape of what he wanted to be careful about, but reading was not the same as a warm hand in yours at the bottom of some steps.

At the car she turned to face him and did not let go of his hand, and he leaned in a little, and she leaned in, and they kissed, briefly, and it was new and good. Then he moved to kiss her again, the way the first one seemed to ask for, and she turned her cheek, gently, and said, "Actually, I'd rather just say goodnight here."

He stepped back at once, and the stepping back felt clumsy in his body even as it was right, and he said, "Of course. Yeah. Goodnight." He heard himself add, too quickly, "That's completely, yeah," and stopped, because the sentence was embarrassing him more than the moment itself had.

"I had a really good time," Nadia said. She was watching his face carefully, the way you watch someone you aren't sure you know yet. "The fish was better than the fish at the restaurant, for the record."

"It was the lemon," Christopher said. "That wasn't even mine."

At the door of his house he stood with his keys in his fist and did not go in right away. He understood, in a way he had not an hour ago, that the yes on the porch and the no ten seconds later were both real and neither canceled the other out, that she could want the first kiss and not the second and that both of those things could be true about the same evening, about the same person, about him even, and that nothing was owed forward from one moment into the next. What he did not know, and could not have known, was whether she would want to see him again, whether the turning of her cheek would turn out to be the end of something or the middle of it. He would have to text her and not know, and wait and not know, which was a kind of not-knowing he had spent his whole life preparing for without ever once practicing.

Chayse was still upstairs, had never left, and called down through the window, "Is she gone? Did it go okay? Come up, tell me everything."

Christopher looked up at the lit window, then back at the empty street where her car had been.

"Bring the leftovers," he called back, and pushed the door open.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
Sophia believed, and had said so twice at dinner, that she was the most honest person in Cabin Four. The evidence was on her side: she had told Aubrey her sunburn looked like a warning label, and she had told the waterfront instructor that his whistle technique was capricious, arriving without pattern, like weather. Honesty, as far as Sophia could tell, was a single substance, like water, and you either offered people a drink or you didn't.

The problem was Alexis. They were paired for the sail regatta on Friday, and Alexis had missed two practice sessions on the water, once for a doctor's appointment and once for no reason anyone could name, and their trapeze work showed it. On Wednesday evening Sophia found her at the picnic table behind the mess hall, carving a point into a popsicle stick for no clear purpose, and Sophia opened her mouth to say what she had been carrying around since the afternoon capsize.

What came out, before she could shape it, was "You always bail on things." She heard it land. Alexis set down the popsicle stick, and her face did a thing Sophia had never seen it do, a closing, like a window in rain, and she said, "Okay," and walked toward the lake with her towel even though it was after hours and the water would be cold.

Sophia sat at the table and tried to reconstruct what had happened, the way you replay a collision. She was sure she had been honest, which was true, and she was fairly sure she had been fair, which was less true, because "always" was a word she had chosen for its weight and not for its accuracy. Alexis had missed practice twice. Twice was a number. Always was a verdict.

Mr. Francis had covered something like this in the psychology elective last spring, and Sophia had half listened from the back row while doodling a sailboat she was now ashamed of. She remembered him writing two words on the board, complaint and criticism, and saying something about a psychologist named Gottman, and she remembered thinking it didn't apply to her because she was honest. She biked to the camp library the next morning, found the unit in her binder, which had survived the drive up in the footwell of her mother's car, and read it twice. A complaint addresses a specific behavior, the notes said. Criticism attacks the person's character. She sat with that for a while, noticing how differently the two sentences were built, like a carpenter noticing that a hinge and a nail are both metal but only one lets a door move.

The distinction invigorated her in a way she distrusted a little, the way any new tool does when you first pick it up and want to use it on everything. She practiced on the paddle instructor, saying "the port-side stroke is late" instead of "you're sloppy," and the change felt like steering with two hands instead of one. But she still didn't know what to do about Alexis, because a cleaner sentence wasn't the same as a repaired one, and she was honest enough now to admit she didn't know whether repair was even on offer.

Friday morning arrived warm and windless, then windy, then warm again. Sophia found Alexis rigging their boat early, alone, which surprised her; she'd expected to have to hunt. "Hey," Sophia said, and then, because she had decided on the walk over that she would name the thing itself, "I said 'you always.' That was criticism. It went after you instead of the thing that actually happened, which is you missed practice twice. That's the complaint. The real one." Alexis kept working the jib halyard, and the rope made its small arguing sound in the block, and then she said, "You practiced that." "I did," Sophia said. "Did the doctor thing go okay?" Alexis's hands slowed on the line. "It was my sister," she said. "Not the appointment. The other day. I'll tell you after."

They didn't win the regatta. They placed third, which in a fleet of five meant something different than it would have in a fleet of twenty, and both of them knew it and neither said it out loud. Afterward, hauling the boat up the beach with the sand pulling at the hull, Alexis told her about the sister, quietly, in pieces, while the lake went flat and then not flat again. Sophia carried the stern and listened and did not offer any verdicts at all. When they set the boat on its rack, Alexis wiped her hands on her shorts and said, "Same partner next year?" and Sophia said, "Ask me after the first practice," and Alexis laughed, and the sound carried over the water toward the empty dock.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: In the balanced equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water.
story:
The gym smelled like hot extension cords and someone's vinegar volcano, and Leah stood behind her folding table with a binder clip pinching her poster flat where the glue had failed. Her project was a hydrogen fuel cell model, the kind she'd assembled from a kit and then taken apart twice because the numbers on her board wouldn't balance. She had claimed that four grams of hydrogen gas would produce thirty-six grams of water. Ms. Whitaker had circled the figure in red pencil and written only, "Check your moles," which sounded like an insult but was apparently chemistry.

She wanted the regional prize badly, and not only for the scholarship money. Her father had told her the adage about how the squeaky wheel gets the grease, meaning she should email the judges, introduce herself, be visible. But Leah had always suspected the quieter truth, that the wheel that understood its own axle got further, and she could not yet say what she understood. Her board had a hole in it shaped exactly like a mole.

Fanny arrived at the table holding a paper boat of nachos from the concession stand, trailing cheese steam. "Daniel's here with his magnet thing," she said. "Also, a man with a clipboard keeps stopping at your board and frowning at the same spot Ms. Whitaker frowned."

"That's comforting."

"It's very specific frowning. Symmetrical to the red circle."

A woman in a laminated judge's badge stopped in front of the board and tapped the equation Leah had copied from the kit manual. "Tell me about this. If I burn hydrogen, what do I actually get?" Leah opened her mouth and heard herself say that hydrogen and oxygen made water, which she knew was true and also, in that moment, useless, like knowing a city existed without a map. The judge waited. Behind her, a junior-high kid at the next table was counting on his fingers, mouthing numbers at his own poster, and his patience made Leah feel both worse and oddly steadied.

"So walk me through the arithmetic," the judge said.

Leah turned to her scratch paper, where she had written the equation the night before and then ignored it. Two hydrogen molecules plus one oxygen molecule. She counted atoms the way the kid beside her was counting, drawing little circles under each symbol, two and two on the left, then one and one and one and one, and the circles lined up. Four hydrogen atoms on each side, two oxygen atoms on each side. It was less like a magic trick than like the moment a Rubik's cube section resolved. She wrote beneath it: two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas, and that forms two moles of water. Then she looked up at her wrong answer, thirty-six grams from four grams, and saw where it had gone crooked.

From Fanny's side of the table, the whole thing looked like Leah had fallen into a trance. She was muttering "eighteen, thirty-six, two times," flipping her pencil between her fingers, and the judge had gone very still in the way adults did when they were deciding whether to be impressed. Fanny set down the nachos so she wouldn't interpose them into history. She could not follow the numbers herself; chemistry was where Fanny went truculent, defending her C+ like territory. But she recognized the expression on Leah's face, the same one from the regional spelling bee in eighth grade, right before Leah spelled "larynx" correctly and then sat down shaking.

"Wait," Leah said. "I said four grams of hydrogen gives thirty-six grams of water, but four grams is only two moles of hydrogen, and the equation says that makes two moles of water, so it's thirty-six grams only if I also have the oxygen. One mole of it. Thirty-two grams of oxygen that I never counted, because it just comes from the air, like it's free." She laughed once, a short startled sound. "I was counting the groceries but not the air I breathed."

The judge smiled at that. "Most people do. The air feels free, so the arithmetic feels optional."

"Air isn't free," Leah said, "it's just unmarked." She pulled out a fresh index card and started over, clean columns, the balanced equation at the top like a doorway she could actually walk through now: two moles of hydrogen, one mole of oxygen, two moles of water, the same numbers she had drawn circles under. At the next table the junior-high kid looked over and said, "That's my equation, I have that one too," with the possessive pride of someone who had counted the same atoms on both sides that morning, and Leah said, "You and me both, then," and felt the gym's whole ridiculous warmth, glue and cheese and ozone, settle into something like an even scale.

Fanny leaned against the table edge, arms crossed, wearing her stubborn look. "So is it fixed? Are you going to win?"

"I don't know if I'll win," Leah said. "But the number's true now, which is different from hoping it was true." She taped the new card over the old figure, pressing the corners down hard, and the tape squeaked against the poster board.

The judge made a small mark on her clipboard and moved on toward the volcanoes. Daniel appeared from the far aisle, carrying his magnet contraption with both arms like a sleeping cat, and asked what he'd missed. Fanny pointed at the corrected card.

Leah smoothed the tape one last time with her thumb and left her hand flat on the board, as if she could hold the number still.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aims to make most of it set in form V, the crystal form that gives shine and snap.
story:
Morgan had ruined Zakary's birthday the week before, and she had decided, over three nights of not sleeping especially well, that restitution would come in chocolate. Not the kind you bought, because bought things felt like money, and money was what she had plenty of and he had none of. She wanted to make it with her hands. So on Saturday she stood in Leah's kitchen with two kilograms of dark couverture and a marble slab borrowed from Leah's mother, and the first batch, spread thin and left to set, came out matte as an old chalkboard, breaking without any sound at all, crumbling between her fingers like wet sand.

"That's not chocolate," Leah said, poking it. "That's dirt with ambition."

Morgan sat on the counter with her phone and read, chewing her lip. Cocoa butter could crystallize in six different forms, the article said, and tempering was the whole art of coaxing most of it into form V, the one crystal form that gave shine and snap. Six forms, one of them right. She read the sentence twice, then said it aloud just to hear whether it could possibly be true.

"Six," Leah said from the stove. "Form five is the good one. Form V. Shine and snap." She stirred the pot she was meant to be watching for her own reasons, which mostly involved not being in her own head. "You have to say the whole thing or you'll forget the number."

"I'm not going to forget the number. I couldn't forget the number if I tried." Morgan hadn't been able to verbalize any of what the week before had actually been, not to Leah, not to Zakary, not to the group chat that had gone quiet in a way she could feel in her chest. Six forms of crystal felt, absurdly, like something she could actually control.

She chopped the second batch small so it would melt evenly, then worked it on the marble with a spatula, spreading and gathering, spreading and gathering, until the shine came up like a tide. Her wrists ached. Leah turned the kitchen radio low and neither of them spoke for a while, and the chocolate made a soft dragging sound against stone, and outside the light went the color of weak tea. When a shard of it set on the back of her hand in under a minute, glossy and cool as something igneous poured from the earth and frozen midflow, Morgan held her breath and snapped it. The crack was clean and loud, like a knuckle, like a small door.

"It worked," she said. "Leah. It actually worked."

"Temper, they call it." Leah leaned over the bars, gray and glossy now in their paper molds, and Morgan could see her own face faintly reflected in the top one. It had taken two hours and a ruined kilogram and every bit of patience she owned, and now she had nine bars that looked bought, that looked professional, that looked like something a competent and thoughtful person would make.
