She wrapped three in parchment and wrote Zakary's name on the paper, and was threading the ribbon through when Leah, who had been quiet at the counter, held up a shard of the failed first batch, the chalky one, the dirt with ambition, and ate it anyway. She chewed slowly. Her eyes closed a little.

"You know," Leah said, "this one tastes better. It's wrong, but it melts faster. It's softer in the mouth." She held out the matte crumbling piece to Morgan, who took it, and it did melt faster, wrong and warm and gone too soon, and she was still deciding which of them was the real chocolate when the doorbell rang, and through the frosted glass she could see it was Zakary, come over unannounced, a day early, already holding a box of her own.

"You'd better hide the good ones," Leah said, and Morgan, with the ribbon half tied, put them behind the breadbin.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: German historian Alexander Demandt compiled a list of 210 different explanations that writers have offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell.
story:
The debate was scheduled for the last period on a Friday, which Ms. Nowak had probably intended as a joke, because nobody argues well at two in the afternoon in June. Isabelle had drawn the position that Rome fell because of barbarian invasions, and she had spent three nights with index cards spread across the kitchen table while her mother asked, from the doorway, whether all that was really due Monday.

"There were barbarian invasions," Shay said now, leaning across the aisle before the bell finished ringing. "That part's just true."

"That's not the point. The point is whether it's the cause." Isabelle shuffled her cards, and her heart began to palpitate in the way it did before she had to speak in front of people, a quick irregular drumming she could feel in her wrists. "There's a difference between something that happened and something that explains it."

Ms. Nowak stood at the board and wrote a single word: FALL. "You each have four minutes," she said. "Then the floor opens. Isabelle, you're first."

Isabelle argued as she had practiced: the Rhine frontier, the Gothic crossings, the sack of the city. She kept her voice level and her eyes on the back wall, and when she sat down she thought she had done well, until Emilio stood up and dismantled the whole thing in ninety seconds. The empire had absorbed barbarians for centuries, he said; whole armies had been staffed by them; blaming the invasions was almost tautological, since every empire that falls has enemies at the end, and every empire that has enemies at the end falls. "It explains nothing," he finished, folding his notes without looking at them. "It just restates the question."

She wanted to object and found she couldn't. Her cards sat in her lap, and one of them, the one with the population figures, seemed suddenly beside the point, a fact with no sentience of its own, unable to testify about why anything had happened.

"Isabelle," Ms. Nowak said, "you may respond."

She stood up without deciding to. "I want to withdraw the argument," she said, and the room went quiet in the way rooms do when someone breaks the script of a Friday debate. "Not because it's wrong. Because I can't defend it alone."

Ms. Nowak tilted her head. "Alone?"

Last summer Isabelle had sat in the public library on Corvane Street, waiting out a thunderstorm, and had pulled a green book off the shelf more for its cracked spine than anything else. It was a survey of the fall of Rome, and in a footnote she had read something that had stayed with her the way certain sentences do: a German historian named Alexander Demandt had collected two hundred and ten different explanations that writers had offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell. She had counted the implications of the number twice on her fingers, and then counted them again. Two hundred and ten. Not theories in the abstract, but actual explanations, each one argued by someone, somewhere, with evidence.

"Say the number again," Shay had said when Isabelle texted her from under the library awning, rain still coming off it in ropes. "Nobody has two hundred and ten of anything."

Now she said it out loud in the classroom. "There's a historian, Demandt, a German. He compiled a list of two hundred and ten explanations that have actually been offered for the fall of the Western Empire. Two hundred and ten. Lead poisoning, Christianity, taxes, weather, decadence, bureaucracy." She looked at Emilio. "So when you say the invasions explain nothing, maybe nothing explains it alone. Maybe the honest answer is that we're each holding one card out of two hundred and ten, and the deck doesn't belong to any of us."

"That's a cop-out," Emilio said, but without heat.

"It might be." She was still standing, and she found she didn't want to sit down yet, which surprised her. "Here's what I actually think. The sources we have are pieces. Some Roman wrote down what he saw, or what he hated, or what he wanted his emperor to hear. Then a monk copied it and maybe changed it. Then somebody in the eighteen hundreds translated it to prove something about their own country. Every one of those people was answering a different question than ours." She put the index cards down on the desk, squared them, and left them there. "And the questions keep changing. People asked why Rome fell to warn their own empire, or their own church, or their own century. We're asking it to get a grade."

A boy near the window laughed, and then stopped when nobody joined him.

"That's not relativism," Ms. Nowak said. "Or it doesn't have to be."

"I know it doesn't have to be." Isabelle thought of the library again, of the rain coming down in the parking lot while she stood with her thumb over her phone, unable to make the number feel real. "Some explanations are better than others. But I can't tell you which ones anymore, and I could yesterday, and that's the part I can't shake."

The bell would ring in six minutes. Ms. Nowak looked at the word FALL on the board, then rubbed part of it out with her thumb, leaving only the letters FA, ambiguous, unfinished.

"Someone take the open floor," she said. "Convince her of something."

Emilio stood up with his notes still folded in his hand. "Pick your card back up," he said. "Barbarians. I'll argue the Christians, and we'll see whose ghost is louder."

Isabelle bent and picked the cards off the desk.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution in his 1863 book on drama technique.
story:
Grandma's bookshelves had a way of handing you exactly the wrong book, which was how Madison found herself blowing dust off a fat green volume titled, in cracked gold letters, Die Technik des Dramas. She had come upstairs looking for a coaster. What she got was Gustav Freytag, 1863, and a Saturday afternoon that would not go as planned.

The drama camp packet lay downstairs on the kitchen table, next to Grandma's puzzle. Ten-minute play, due in nine days, "drawn from a moment in your own life." Ms. Korhonen had said it with the flat cheer of someone assigning something she knew would hurt. Madison had a moment, all right. She had several. The problem was that her moment refused to have a shape.

She sat cross-legged on the attic rug and worked through the German with her phone and her two semesters of duolingo streak. Somewhere around page ninety she stopped translating word by word, because the diagram on the page was doing the work for her. Freytag had drawn the structure of drama as a pyramid. Exposition at the base, rising action climbing one slope, the climax at the peak, then falling action descending, and resolution at the far corner.

"He drew it as a pyramid," she said out loud, to the attic, to the dead man. "In 1863. A whole book on drama technique and he drew a pyramid."

At camp on Monday, Ms. Korhonen distributed napkins with the coffee because the camp was run out of a church hall that had run out of everything else. Elyane claimed two napkins and a handful of sugar packets, because Elyane's play was going to be about her parents' divorce and she intended to survive the writing of it through snacks. Sunny wanted to write about the time he got locked in the planetarium overnight, and he wanted, more than anything, for the camp's final showcase to pick his play for the regional festival, and he said so constantly, so no one could accidentally steal the dream without knowing it was taken.

Madison drew the pyramid on her napkin. Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution, labeled in ballpoint. Then she tried to locate her moment on it. The moment was this: two winters ago, Grandma had been in the hospital for eleven days, and Madison, seventeen and terrified in a way she had refused to name, had told her mother she had a debate tournament and could not visit. There had been no tournament. She had watched four seasons of a show about chefs instead, and Grandma had come home anyway, thinner, and had never once asked about the tournament.

She kept trying to put the lie at the top of the pyramid, and it kept sliding down the slopes. Was the lie the climax? Or was the climax the hospital, which Madison had no scenes for because she hadn't been there? She drew arrows. She crossed out arrows. Sunny leaned over and said, "Your napkin looks like a cult diagram," and she said, "It's sectarian, actually, me against Freytag," and Elyane laughed so hard a sugar packet went down her shirt.

That night, back at Grandma's, Madison went through the green book again and found something tucked between pages 112 and 113: an envelope, her own handwriting on it, aged two winters. She had forgotten writing it. She had forgotten it so completely that opening it felt like shoplifting from herself.

Dear Grandma, the letter said. I don't have a tournament. I'm scared you're going to die and I don't want the last thing to be a hospital room with you small in the bed. I had a presentiment all week, like the air before snow, and I couldn't. I'm sorry. I'll tell you in person. Love, Madison.

She had never told her in person. The letter had gone into the wrong book, or the right one, and had desiccated there between the rising action and the falling action, waiting.

Madison carried the letter downstairs. Grandma was at the kitchen table sorting puzzle pieces by color, which she claimed was strategy and everyone else knew was avoidance. Madison set the envelope by the blue pieces. Grandma read it without hurrying, the way she did everything, then folded it once and put it under the sugar bowl.

"That was the resolution," Madison said. "Of the play. I couldn't find it because it hadn't happened yet."

"That's not how plays work, is it," Grandma said. "Resolution at the end. This one took you the middle."

On the ninth day, in the church hall, Elyane read the mother's part and Sunny read the nurse and Ms. Korhonen stood by the coffee urn with her arms folded. The play was ten minutes: a girl, a lie, a hospital she never entered, a pyramid the narrator drew in the air with one finger. At the showcase they picked Sunny's planetarium play for the festival, and Sunny apologized with his whole face while radiating joy, and Madison found she didn't mind, or minded only the ordinary amount.

Grandma took the green book home on the bus with her, tucked under her coat. "I'm keeping Gustav," she said. "He's family now."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: A Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, noticing servants and workers the novel mentions only in passing.
story:
Hudson had claimed the table by the window at the public library for two hours, and the paperback copy of Jane Eyre had been open to chapter seventeen for most of that time, though he had read the same paragraphs four times without any of them sticking. The assignment sheet lay beside it, creased from being folded and unfolded in his pocket. Ms. Lin wanted a critical lens applied to a single chapter, and she had listed them on the board like menu options: feminist, Marxist, postcolonial, psychoanalytic. Hudson had circled Marxist because Ilan had said it was the easiest, and Ilan's judgment on such matters had never yet been wrong, though Ilan also had a habit of finishing his essays at lunch on the day they were due.

Across the table, Ilan was watching a video with one earbud in, which meant he was half available. "You still on the same page?" he said, not looking up.

"I don't know what I'm looking for," Hudson said. "Like, I know it's supposed to be about class, but the chapter's about a party at Thornfield. There's literally nothing about class in it."

Ilan pulled out the earbud. "That's the whole thing, though. It's about class when it looks like it isn't." He said this with the confidence of someone repeating something he had heard rather than tested, and went back to his video.

Hudson flipped the page over. The party was in full swing: guests arrived, elegantly dressed, trading wit about the governess in the room. He had underlined the word governess six times already, which felt like progress but probably wasn't. The guests performed charades; Rochester was magnetic; Blanche Ingram was beautiful and terrible. He wrote "gender roles?" in the margin, then scratched it out, because that was the other lens, the feminist one, and Ms. Lin had said the lenses could not simply be swapped halfway through like interchangeable screwdrivers.

He started counting, more out of boredom than method. It was something his mother did with receipts, this habit of tallying, and his hand did it before his brain agreed. There were footmen mentioned, and a maid named Leah, and a housekeeper, Mrs. Fairfax, hovering at the edges of the scene. He made a small column in the back of his notebook. The servants appeared, by his count, eleven times in the chapter. Then he made a second column, for how many times any of them spoke. He went back through the pages slowly, running a finger under each line, and the second column came to two, and one of those was only Mrs. Fairfax saying that supper was ready.

He sat back. The party glittered on the page, and beneath it, holding the whole thing up, were people the novel mentioned only in passing, carrying trays and stoking fires and vanishing into doorways. Nobody at the party wondered whose labour kept the candles lit. Nobody, which was the point, because the novel itself didn't wonder either, not once. He wrote at the top of his notebook, "A Marxist reading asks whose labour makes these comfortable lives possible," and it wasn't a thesis yet, but it was a hinge, and things could swing on a hinge.

Thomas arrived at four with a chess set and no intention of studying. He dropped into the third chair, began setting up pieces, and asked what Hudson had. Hudson read him the two columns, the eleven and the two, and Thomas frowned at the numbers as though they were a move he hadn't anticipated.

"So your whole essay is, like, the servants don't talk much?"

"It's not that simple," Hudson said, though he could feel how it might sound that way, like a trick with a tally. "The feminist lens is sitting right there too. Jane's in that room being scrutinized by people who have power over her because she's a woman without money. Both things are true at once. The class system and the way the women in it get sorted. I think I can hold both."

"Sounds like twice the work," Thomas said, and moved a pawn.

Ms. Lin came by near closing to collect returned books from the drop bin, and she paused at their table long enough to see the notebook. She read the two columns, and then the sentence at the top, and Hudson braced for the verdict. Some teachers eviscerated a half-formed idea in a single scathing comment, and he had watched it happen to other people's essays often enough to fear the artifice of his own counting, the possibility that he had dressed up a simple tally as insight.

"Where did the second column come from?" she asked.

"Me. I just started counting and then I couldn't stop noticing them. They're everywhere once you look. And they almost never open their mouths."

She set the notebook down. "Keep both lenses. Let them argue with each other on the page." Then she went on toward the bins, pushing the cart ahead of her.

Hudson looked at the chessboard, where Thomas was already losing to Ilan in six moves, and then back at the chapter, at Leah carrying something up the stairs and out of the novel entirely. He underlined her name once, gently, and turned the page.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism was based on only twelve children.
story:
The writing club met on Thursdays in the library's back room, where the radiators clanked and nobody could hear you fail. Brody set his laptop on the table, opened the folder Ms. Qureshi had shared, and waited for the others to stop arguing about the vending machine. The assignment was a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, and he had chosen, at midnight two days earlier, two articles about the vaccine-autism controversy. He regretted the choice already, and also suspected it was the most honest thing he had ever picked.

"Yours is depressing," Shayla said, reading over his shoulder before he could tilt the screen away. "Mine's about whether music training improves memory. Yours is about a scandal."

"It's not a scandal, it's a question," Brody said. "Two articles answering the same question differently. That's the whole assignment."

Fletcher dropped into the chair across from them, unwrapping a granola bar with the ceremony of someone who considered lunch optional. "Which question, though? Because if the two articles are answering two different questions and just pretending they're the same one, that's the actual problem. That happens more than you'd think." He said this with the confidence of a person who had learned it from a podcast, but Brody wrote it down anyway.

Ms. Qureshi came around with the signup sheet and paused at his screen. "Brody, are you comparing the articles or are you adjudicating them?" He did not know what she meant, and he disliked how obviously his face showed it. She tapped the table twice, her signal for think about it, and moved on to the girl writing about climate migration.

He read the first article again while Shayla argued with Fletcher about whether her music studies were "penurious little sample sizes" or reasonable ones; she won, mostly by making him look up the word. The article he kept rereading was a history of the controversy, and it was the second article, a review of the evidence, that had enthralled him at midnight, though he could not yet say why. Something about the two pieces didn't line up, and the mismatch was under the sentences, not in them. He scrolled back to a page he had highlighted in yellow without understanding, and then it surfaced, small and plain as a coin at the bottom of a pool.

"Twelve," he said out loud.

Shayla looked up. "What?"

"The original paper. Wakefield's, 1998, in The Lancet, claiming MMR was linked to autism. It was based on twelve children." He turned the laptop so they could see. "Twelve. And the review article is looking at studies with thousands of kids, and that's why they disagree. Not because somebody's lying. Because one of them is standing on a pebble and calling it a mountain." Fletcher stopped chewing. He leaned over, read the number, read it again, and said, "Twelve," in a different voice than before, as if the word had changed weight between them.

Brody sat with it for a moment, and a memory arrived without invitation: his mother, years ago, at the kitchen table with a printout she would not let him see, deciding something about his little brother's shots over three long evenings. He had been twelve himself then, and he had thought the decision was about belief. Now he understood it had been about evidence, and about which evidence she had been handed. He did not know whether that made her wrong or merely badly served, and he noticed that the review article did not settle it either, because a review can tell you what the studies found but not what fear does to a person reading them alone at a kitchen table.

He began to type. The draft came out crooked, half review and half something else, an argument that the two articles were not really opponents but a counterpoint, one describing what the evidence said and the other describing why the evidence had been drowned out. He kept stopping. He could hear Ms. Qureshi's question again, are you comparing or adjudicating, and he still did not have an answer, only the suspicion that honesty might mean saying so in the paper itself, in a sentence like: the record supports one conclusion; the reasons the record was doubted deserve their own accounting. He showed Shayla the paragraph. She read it twice.

"That's not really a conclusion," she said.

"I know."

"Are you going to fix it?"

He looked at the paragraph, at the twelve sitting in the middle of it like a stone in a shoe, and then at the door, where his mother would be waiting in the car at five, the same woman who had printed out that article four years ago and never mentioned it again. "I don't think so," he said, and kept typing.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The world's first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was founded in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
The community food bank had been set up in the lecture hall of the public library, since the library had the only loading dock on the street, and Oliver arrived at nine with a form his mother had signed and a suspicion that he had agreed to this only to have something to write in his college applications. Edmond was already there, stacking canned peaches with the concentration of someone defusing them. Konnor had not come at all, though he had been the one to find the listing.

Ms. Sun, who ran the Saturday distribution, gave Oliver a pallet jack and one instruction: the expired goods go on the left table, the good goods go on the right, and the expired goods are still legal, still edible, still going home with people. "You'll want to hide them," she said. "Everyone does. Don't."

He worked the aisles for an hour. The hall smelled of cardboard and the floor wax the library used, and through the open doors he could hear the checkout desk beeping in the distance, that small polite sound repeating while he sorted dented soup from undented. A man at the far table, waiting for his number to be called, watched Oliver work with what he first took for suspicion and then decided was simply boredom.

Near the loading dock, a laminated poster had been taped to the rolling shelf, curling at the corners. Oliver read it while he waited for the elevator. The world's first food bank, it said, was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, founded in 1967 by John van Hengel. He read it twice. He had assumed food banks were ancient, like poorhouses, or very new, like the recycling bins outside his school. Sixty years, roughly, was all. Someone had thought of it, one man, in one desert city, and now there was this folding table in a library in a town van Hengel had never heard of.

He told Edmond this over the plastic-wrapped sandwiches. Edmond said, "Who cares," which was Edmond's version of interest. Oliver cared in a way he couldn't quite locate. He had come in truculent, he could admit that to himself, angry in a low flat way at his mother for making him go, at Konnor for vanishing, at the whole arrangement by which he, Oliver, who had a car and a meal plan waiting in August, would hand a stranger a bag of near-expired rice. The history poster did not absolve him of that feeling. It just made the feeling smaller and stranger. Someone had stood where he was standing, once, without a poster on the wall to tell him what it would become.

At eleven a woman came through with two children, took a number, and sat down in the row of chairs that was normally the library's reading area. Her son, maybe seven, pulled a picture book off the returns cart and read it upside down, then right side up, then upside down again, deciding something about it. When the woman's number was called, Oliver packed her bag, and he hesitated over a box of granola bars that was two days past its date. He put it in. Then he took it out. Then he put it in again and slid a second box on top, unexpired, so she wouldn't have to choose or notice or explain anything to her children. It was a small act of hiding, exactly the thing Ms. Sun had told him not to do, and he did it anyway, and then stood there holding the bag while she waited.

Konnor arrived at noon, out of breath, apologizing about a bus that had never come. Oliver gave him the expired table, and Konnor worked it without complaint, and when Oliver mentioned Phoenix, 1967, a man named John van Hengel, Konnor stopped, looked at the poster for a long moment, and said, "Huh. I figured it was, like, a church thing from forever." Konnor had spent the whole morning before arriving saying the whole exercise was charity theater, bathos in boxes, sad music with no soundtrack. Now he was arranging expired pasta by shape.

At the end of the shift Ms. Sun collected the clipboards and asked Oliver whether he'd be back. He said probably, and meant it, though he still didn't know whether he was doing it for the applicants' column or for the woman with the picture book, or whether that distinction would survive another Saturday. He carried the last two boxes toward the loading dock, and the elevator opened, and inside it stood the man from the far table, holding a bag of groceries and a library book on fixing small engines, and the man looked at Oliver's boxes, then at the open doors behind him, and said, "You going down? Press two."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide.
story:
The nature trail behind the school had three benches, and Sienna had claimed the one nearest the creek because, she said, the white noise of water helped her think. It did not help Angelina think. It made her want to pee, which she mentioned twice before Callen told her to open her textbook and stop narrating her bladder. The exam was Monday. It was Saturday. Between them they had one bag of trail mix, one phone with eleven percent battery, and one genuine dispute about cellular respiration, which was, in Angelina's private opinion, the worst kind of dispute because nobody could win it by being louder.

"Pyruvate oxidation," Callen said, tapping the diagram with a sunflower seed. "That's where the first carbon dioxide comes off. Pyruvate goes into the matrix and gets converted to acetyl-CoA, and each pyruvate releases one molecule of CO2. One. That's the step."

Sienna shook her head with the weary patience of someone who had been wrong once already that week and did not intend to be wrong again. "The link reaction isn't the answer to the question. The question is which step makes the first carbon dioxide, and I think it's the Krebs cycle, because that's where all the CO2 everybody talks about shows up. Four per glucose. That's the famous number."

"Famous," Angelina repeated. "You said a number in cellular respiration was famous."

"It is famous within this bench."

Angelina sat between them with the book open across her knees and felt the familiar pressure of two people she liked saying two different things with equal certainty. Her instinct, historically, was to prevaricate, to say something like "it probably depends on how you look at it," which had gotten her through four years of group projects and exactly zero moments of actual learning. But the creek kept going, and the exam kept approaching, and somewhere in the back of her mind a diagram from Mr. Wright's slides floated up, the one with the little arrow crossing into the mitochondrion.

She found it. Page 171, a drawing she had copied into her notes without understanding, and now she understood it, or at least she could read it, and reading it felt suspiciously like understanding. "Wait," she said, and both of them stopped arguing because Angelina saying "wait" in that tone was a rare event. "Look at the order. Glycolysis happens first, in the cytoplasm, and there's no CO2 there at all. Then pyruvate enters the matrix. In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide." She moved her finger along the arrow. "So by the time the Krebs cycle even starts, CO2 has already come off. Two molecules, actually, one from each pyruvate. Callen's right. The first one."

Callen did not gloat, which Angelina noted and filed away as evidence of his character. Sienna stared at the page for a long moment, then leaned back against the bench and addressed the trees. "So I've had it backwards since October."

"Since October," Callen confirmed.

"Thank you for the precise dating."

"That's what friends are for."

Angelina closed the book on her finger to hold the page. What she noticed, sitting there, was that she hadn't picked a side so much as gone and looked, and that looking had produced something better than an opinion. She also noticed she still couldn't explain why the carbon came off, only that it did, and she said so, because pretending otherwise seemed like a good way to fail Monday. "I can tell you where it happens," she said. "I can't tell you why yet. Is that enough?"

"For the exam, probably," Sienna said. "For the rest of it, no. But you have until Monday to be a person who knows things partially."

There was a Saturnine old man walking a saturnine old dog farther down the trail, both of them regarding the study group as if youth itself were a personal affront, and when the dog stopped to investigate Callen's backpack the man said nothing, just waited, then moved on like a cloud passing. Angelina watched them go and thought, briefly, of Mr. Wright, who would be grading the exam with that same expression and who would, she suspected, be quietly pleased that the three of them were out here on a Saturday, on a bench, arguing about a molecule.

"We should do this again," Sienna said. "Not the arguing. The bench."

"The bench is the arguing," Callen said. He shook the trail mix bag, found it empty, and looked into it with the betrayed expression of a man receiving a verdict he had not earned. Angelina had no sympathy; he had eaten the M&Ms first, which in her moral system forfeited any claim to acquittal, whatever the remaining evidence suggested. She stood, brushed sunflower salt off her jeans, and held out her hand for the phone so she could photograph page 171 before the battery died. "Say matrix," she said, and took the picture.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
story:
Jordan had claimed the table by the window on the second floor of the public library, the one with the afternoon light that nobody else seemed to want, and spread out his materials like a surgeon arranging instruments: a canvas board, a magazine he had already begun to cut apart, a pot of glue gone slightly moribund at the rim, and a photograph of his grandmother's farm that he had been carrying around for three weeks without using. The assignment, due Friday for the community studio's youth show, was a landscape collage. He knew what the photograph wanted to become. He did not yet know how to make it happen.

Katerina dropped her bag across from him and began peeling the label off her water bottle, which was her way of settling in. She looked at his arrangement of torn paper fields and the flat grey strip he intended for a sky, and she reached over and slid the horizon line upward with one finger. "Put it a third of the way down," she said. "Or a third of the way up, if you want more land. Rule of thirds."

"Who made that a rule?" Jordan asked, not to be difficult but because the question had risen in him almost before she finished speaking. His art teacher in middle school had said the same thing, horizon at a third, subject off-centre, as though reciting something fixed. He had followed it then. Now the grey strip sat at the exact middle of his board and he could not decide whether that was a mistake or a choice.

"Some dead painter, probably," Katerina said. "Nobody knows. It's just old."

That was not good enough for Jordan, and he told her so. She shrugged, said the library had art books downstairs, and went back to her label. He left his materials to guard the table and went down.

The art section was two shelves of sun-faded spines, and for a while it yielded nothing but coffee-table books that assumed he already knew what he wanted to know. Then, in a thick volume on composition, he found a footnote that stopped him. The phrase "rule of thirds," the small print said, was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book, Remarks on Rural Scenery. He read the sentence twice. Not invented then, not born then. Written down. Smith had put into words something people had perhaps been doing for years, and afterwards it had hardened into instruction, a rule passed along by teachers who had never heard of the man.

He carried the volume back upstairs. The light had moved; his collage papers lay in a warm parallelogram across the table. He sat down and did not pick up the glue.

"Find it?" Katerina asked.

"The rule of thirds was first written down by John Thomas Smith," Jordan said, "in 1797, in a book called Remarks on Rural Scenery."

"Never heard of him."

"Nobody has. That's the point." He turned the farm photograph so she could see it, the fence line running dead level through the centre of the frame, exactly where his grandmother had stood and pointed the camera without hesitation. "He wrote it down and now everybody repeats it like it's physics. But it's one man's observation. It's a suggestion that got old enough to seem like a law."

Katerina considered this, chewing the corner of the label she had finally freed. "So put the horizon in the middle," she said. "On purpose."

"It looks bad in the middle."

"So it's a good suggestion," she said, laughing, and he had to admit the argument was fair. That was the trouble. He wanted to be an iconoclast about it, to break the rule loudly and feel the satisfaction of refusing, but the photograph kept telling him the fence wanted to sit lower, the sky wanted room. Rebelling against something that happened to be right felt like cutting off his nose. And obeying it without thinking felt like a smaller kind of failure, quieter, harder to notice.

He worked through the last of the afternoon light. First he tried the horizon at a third from the top, and the collage immediately looked composed, deliberate, better in a way he distrusted because it had cost him nothing. Then he tried the middle again and sat with it, really looking, and it did look worse, though he caught himself wondering whether it looked worse because it was worse or because he had been trained to see it that way, and he could not untangle the two, and suspected nobody could. In the end he set the horizon just below the centre, close enough to the rule that a viewer might credit him with knowing it, far enough that he had not simply obeyed. He glued it down before he could reconsider.

Katerina leaned over to inspect it. "So is that you agreeing with Smith or arguing with him?"

"I honestly don't know," Jordan said. He pressed the edge of the paper flat with his thumb and watched the glue squeeze out along the fence line like frost.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared.
story:
The math club met on Tuesdays in Room 114, where the radiator clanked and the chalkboard still held the ghost of last week's proof. Jordyn arrived early because she wanted the seat by the window, and because Chaya had texted her the night before in a panic about the problem set. Chaya's messages were always like that, all lowercase, no punctuation, and Jordyn had read this one three times on the bus: derivative problems due tomorrow and i don't get why my numbers are wrong. Tom was already there, eating a granola bar with his feet on the chair in front of him, and Mr. Szabó was at his desk pretending not to watch the clock.

Chaya spread her homework across two desks like evidence at a trial. Eight problems, polynomials mostly, and beside each one a derivative in her round, careful handwriting. Jordyn leaned over her shoulder and checked the first one against the formula sheet. Chaya had a function with x cubed in it, and she had written 3x cubed as the derivative, dragging the exponent down whole instead of changing it.

"You dropped the power rule," Jordyn said.

"What rule?"

"It's called the power rule," Jordyn said, tapping the sheet. "The derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1." She read it slowly, the way she'd read it to herself on the bus until it stopped sounding like words. "So the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared. You kept the three but you didn't lower the power."

Chaya looked at her page as if it had betrayed her personally. Jordyn understood the feeling. For most of the semester she had treated differentiation as a kind of ritual, steps performed in order for reasons nobody had made plain to her, and it had worked the way a spell works, until it didn't. The power rule was the first piece that had started to feel less like a spell and more like a door.

"Every single one?" Chaya said, flipping through the pages. She found a problem with x to the fifth and wrote 5x to the fourth beside it, then another, then another, correcting down the line. Jordyn slid her own notebook over so Chaya could compare, and Tom wandered over, brushing crumbs off his jeans, and said the word "detractor" by accident instead of "derivative," which made Chaya laugh for the first time all afternoon and Jordyn laugh so hard she had to put her pencil down. Tom defended himself. "A detractor is a critic," he said. "I have many. They're evanescent, though. They fade when I get the answer right."

Mr. Szabó came over with his coffee and stood behind them without saying anything, which was his way of saying everything was fine. Then he wrote one problem on the board: a polynomial, negative x squared plus eight x plus something, and beneath it the word MAXIMUM. "Club challenge," he said. "First pair to locate the maximum wins the leftover pretzels." He set the bag on his desk and walked away, because he never explained anything if he could avoid it.

Jordyn took the derivative the way she'd shown Chaya, and got negative 2x plus 8. Tom, still muttering that his critics were ephemeral and also evanescent, insisted they should graph it by hand, plot a dozen points, draw the curve, and read the peak off the picture. Chaya wanted to plug in numbers and hunt around. Jordyn sat between them with her pencil still warm from the power rule and thought about what the derivative actually meant to her, which was that it told you the slope at a single point, and a maximum was where the slope went flat, where it touched zero without quite belonging to either side. The two approaches weren't enemies. She set negative 2x plus 8 equal to zero, got x equals 4, and then, because Tom had a point about evidence, told him to check it. He plotted the points around it, and there was the peak, exactly where her algebra said, the curve rising and turning and falling like a hill seen from a window.

"We're not splitting the pretzels three ways," Chaya said, already reaching for the bag, and Mr. Szabó raised his cup to them without looking up from his crossword.

Walking out later into the cold, Jordyn turned the idea over the way she turned everything over, half trusting it, half waiting for it to fail her somewhere down the road, in some chapter she hadn't reached yet, where the rule might break or bend. Chaya bumped her shoulder and said thanks, and asked whether the power rule worked on things that weren't polynomials, and Jordyn said she didn't know yet.

"Let's find out Thursday," Chaya said, and pushed open the door to the parking lot, where the streetlights were just coming on.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Frida Kahlo's The Two Fridas (1939) is a large, nearly square oil painting, about 173 centimetres on each side, showing two seated self-portraits side by side.
story:
The projector hummed in the art barn like a wasp trapped under a cup, and Mr. Adeyemi kept smacking its side until The Two Fridas swam into focus on the wall. Katherine sat in the second row with her notebook open, pen hovering, and wrote nothing, because the assignment was to say something out loud tomorrow and she had never in her life critiqued a painting. She had critiqued her mother's parking, her brother's haircut, and the camp's chili, but never a painting.

"It's huge," Farhan whispered from the seat behind her. "How huge, do you think? Bigger than my dorm fridge?"

"Everything is bigger than your dorm fridge. You keep a single yogurt in there." Kristian leaned over Katherine's shoulder. "You could live inside that painting. You could sublet it."

Mr. Adeyemi clapped twice. "Tomorrow, formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Not whether you like it. Whether it works, and how you know." He clicked the projector off, and the two Fridas vanished, and Katherine felt the peculiar panic of a blank page being assigned before the page existed.

That evening she found the art history section of the camp library, which was a shelf in the back of the crafts cabin, wedged between the glue gun and a bin of feathers. There was a catalogue with a plate of the painting, and measurements printed beneath it in small type. She read them twice, then measured with her hands, then made Farhan lie down on the cabin floor, arms over his head.

"What are you doing," he said, from the floor.

"Hold still. I'm doing science." She walked heel to toe along him, counting under her breath, and arrived at a number that made her sit down hard on a crate of feathers. "Farhan. It's nearly square. About 173 centimetres on each side. That's you, basically. You are the size of this painting."

Farhan sat up and looked at the side of his own arm as if it might have opinions. "I've never been a unit of measurement before. I feel celebrated."

"You should. Two Fridas sit side by side on a canvas your size. Seated. Both of them." She was flipping the catalogue back to the plate, talking faster now. "That's why she fills the whole thing. There's no room around them, there's no landscape that matters, it's just two women and this enormous sky and they take up everything."

Kristian, who had wandered in looking for the glue gun, drifted over. "So the composition is the argument. They fill the square because the painting is about being filled by yourself. Twice."

"Maybe." Katherine frowned at the plate. The Frida on the left held scissors and an exposed heart; the Frida on the right held a small portrait. "Or maybe it's simpler than that and we're litigating a feeling that isn't there. Mr. Adeyemi says symbolism can be a trap. You see a heart, you decide it means heartbreak, and then you build a whole case like a lawyer with one witness."

"Then build a better case," Kristian said. "You've got colour. One's in white, one's in that ridiculous blue, and they're holding hands in the middle like they're both too proud to admit it."

Farhan squinted. "The white one's heart is cut open and the sky's all stormy behind her. The blue one's heart's intact and the sky's calmer. So is that causality or coincidence? Does the storm cause the bleeding, or is the sky just being dramatic?"

"That's the wrong question," Katherine said, and then stopped, because she wasn't sure it was. "Or it's a good question asked wrongly. Maybe the sky doesn't cause anything. Maybe it agrees with her." She wrote agreeable sky in her notebook, crossed it out, wrote weather as witness, crossed that out too, and left a small blank square in the middle of the page.

She spent the walk back to her cabin arguing it aloud to nobody, or rather to the two of them, who had appointed themselves her rehearsal audience and kept interrupting. "Say the part about the blood again," Farhan said. "You said the blood is white because it's not blood, it's paint, and she's showing you she made herself, both selves, out of the same material. That part was good. Say it exactly like that tomorrow."

"I said it better the first time. That's the problem with saying things."

At breakfast Mr. Adeyemi passed their table and paused, coffee in hand. "Katherine. Ready?" and she said, "Mostly," which was, she decided, the only honest answer available, because she had a case about the square canvas and the two seated figures filling it, a case about white dress and blue dress, about a heart cut open and a heart held closed, and no verdict on whether the sky meant anything at all.

When her turn came, she stood in front of the projection, and Farhan, in the back row, raised his hand solemnly and announced to the room, "For scale, she measured me. I am the painting."
